projects/booru-image-downloader/guides/r.content:
Rule34 Tag Watcher: The Doomsday File
This is the file for Future Me, Curious You, or Whoever Is Staring At A Dead Drive At 2 A.M.
It explains what the watcher does, how to install it from nothing, how the storage trick works, how to recover it, and how to unstick Windows Task Scheduler when it decides to become a cryptid.
The short version: this is a Windows Python downloader for exact Rule34 tags. It checks for new posts on a schedule, can backfill all available history, and uses NTFS hard links so one post can appear in several tag folders without storing several physical copies.
What you need

Windows 10 or 11
Python 3.10 or newer from python.org
An NTFS drive for the archive
A Rule34 account, numeric user ID, and API key
The project files from this repository or the release ZIP
Enough free space for the inevitable consequences of your decisions

The watcher uses only Python’s standard library. You do not need pip.
What the finished archive looks like
Rule34 Tag Archive\
├── Copyright\
│   └── example_series\
├── Character\
│   └── example_character\
├── Artist\
│   └── example_artist\
├── General\
│   └── example_general_tag\
└── .r34-watcher\
    ├── files\
    │   └── ...one canonical copy of every post...
    ├── state.sqlite3
    └── watcher.lock
The visible category files and the canonical file are NTFS hard links. They are multiple names for the same physical bytes.
Do not delete .r34-watcher. It contains the canonical file links and the database that remembers what happened.
The five-minute clean install
1. Install Python
Install Python 3.10 or newer from python.org. During setup, enable the option that adds Python to PATH or installs the py launcher.
Open Command Prompt and confirm:
py -3 --version
If py is unavailable, try:
python --version
2. Get the project
Download the repository as a ZIP and extract it somewhere permanent, or clone it:
git clone github.com/ToastSweat/r34-tag-watcher.git
cd r34-tag-watcher
Do not run the watcher from inside a ZIP. Do not schedule it from a temporary Downloads folder unless you enjoy leaving traps for yourself.
3. Get Rule34 API credentials
Log into Rule34, open the account options page, and generate an API key.
The site may display a fragment resembling:
&api_key=ABC123&user_id=456789
The configuration needs only the values:
"user_id": "456789",
"api_key": "ABC123"
Do not include user_id=, api_key=, &, or the combined URL fragment.
Never commit config.json. It contains the API key in plain text because the unattended task must be able to read it.
4. Run setup
Open PowerShell in the extracted project folder and run:
powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\setup.ps1
Setup asks for:

Archive destination
Copyright tags
Character tags
Artist tags
General tags
Check interval
Numeric user ID
API key

Enter tags exactly as the site displays them. Use underscores, not spaces. Separate multiple tags with commas.
Setup writes config.json, checks that the archive drive supports hard links, and installs a scheduled task named Rule34 Tag Watcher.
5. Test it visibly
Double-click:
run_now.bat
Or run it from Command Prompt:
run_now.bat
The first normal run downloads the newest 25 posts for each tag by default. Older results in the scanned pages become a baseline so the hourly watcher can concentrate on new posts.
6. Download history if wanted
Double-click:
run_backfill.bat
Backfill walks every available API page for every configured tag. It is safe to interrupt and rerun. Completed work is skipped, baseline entries are revisited, and overlapping posts receive more hard links rather than more downloaded copies.
Popular tags can take a very long time. Leave the one-second request delay alone unless you have a compelling reason to annoy the API.
Manual configuration
If you do not want to use setup, copy config.example.json to config.json and edit it:
{
  "output_directory": "D:\\Rule34 Tag Archive",
  "api": {
    "base_url": "api.rule34.xxx/index.php",
    "user_id": "456789",
    "api_key": "ABC123"
  },
  "watched_tags": {
    "copyright": ["example_series"],
    "character": ["example_character"],
    "artist": ["example_artist"],
    "general": ["example_general_tag"]
  },
  "schedule": {
    "interval_minutes": 60
  },
  "scan": {
    "results_per_page": 100,
    "pages_per_check": 3,
    "first_run_download_limit_per_tag": 25,
    "max_downloads_per_tag_per_run": 100,
    "request_delay_seconds": 1.0,
    "request_timeout_seconds": 45,
    "retry_attempts": 3
  },
  "downloads": {
    "allowed_extensions": [".jpg", ".jpeg", ".png", ".gif", ".webp"],
    "save_sidecar_metadata": false
  }
}
Add .mp4 and .webm to allowed_extensions before backfill if videos are wanted too.
Validate the configuration and hard-link support without contacting the site:
py -3 .\r34_tag_watcher.py --config .\config.json --check-config
Preview destinations without downloading:
py -3 .\r34_tag_watcher.py --config .\config.json --dry-run
The deduplication trick
Each post is downloaded into:
.r34-watcher\files\<two-character-shard>\<post-id>_<hash>.<extension>
The watcher then calls the operating system’s hard-link function for every matching tag destination.
That gives us all three properties we wanted:

Every tag folder contains ordinary browsable files.
A post can appear under several tags.
The file data consumes space once.

Useful facts:

Hard links must live on the same filesystem volume.
The archive destination must support them; on Windows that normally means NTFS.
Deleting one tag link does not destroy the bytes while another hard link still exists.
Explorer’s folder Properties may count every path and exaggerate used space.
The drive’s free-space change is the reliable measure of physical storage use.
A normal cross-drive copy usually dereferences the links and creates full duplicates.

Installing, checking, and removing the scheduled task
Install or reinstall it from Command Prompt or PowerShell:
powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\install_task.ps1
Verify it from Command Prompt:
schtasks /Query /TN "Rule34 Tag Watcher" /V /FO LIST
Verify it from PowerShell:
Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName "Rule34 Tag Watcher"
Get-ScheduledTask is a PowerShell command. Command Prompt will say it is not recognized if you paste it there without launching PowerShell. That does not mean the task is broken.
Remove only the task:
powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\uninstall_task.ps1
Removing the task does not delete the archive, configuration, database, or logs.
Moving the project or archive
There are two different things:

The project folder contains the Python and launcher scripts.
The archive folder contains the media, hard links, and SQLite state.

If the project folder moves, the scheduled task still points at the old absolute path. Changing config.json is not enough. Remove the old task before the move and reinstall it from the new project folder afterward.
Safe project-folder move:

Run uninstall_task.ps1 from the old project folder.
Move the project folder.
Update output_directory only if the archive also moved.
Run install_task.ps1 from the new project folder.
Run run_now.bat once and check the log.

Moving the archive to another drive is more delicate. A normal Explorer copy can turn every hard link into a separate physical file. Until a dedicated migration tool exists, the safest space-efficient choices are:

Start a fresh archive on the new NTFS drive and run backfill again, or
Use a proven hard-link-aware backup/migration tool and verify the result before deleting the source.

Never delete the source archive until the destination has been verified. Check matching files with:
fsutil hardlink list "D:\Rule34 Tag Archive\Character\some_tag\some_file.jpg"
The output should include both the visible tag path and a path under .r34-watcher\files on the same volume.
Fixing “Another watcher run is already in progress”
The watcher creates:
<archive>\.r34-watcher\watcher.lock
That stops the scheduled check and a manual backfill from modifying the database at the same time.
First, see whether the scheduled task is actually running:
Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName "Rule34 Tag Watcher" | Select-Object TaskName, State
If it says Running, let it finish. A backfill may genuinely take hours.
If it is stuck and you intentionally want to stop it:
Disable-ScheduledTask -TaskName "Rule34 Tag Watcher"
Stop-ScheduledTask -TaskName "Rule34 Tag Watcher" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "Name='python.exe' OR Name='pythonw.exe' OR Name='py.exe'" |
  Where-Object { $_.CommandLine -like '*r34_tag_watcher.py*' } |
  ForEach-Object { Stop-Process -Id $_.ProcessId -Force }
Only after confirming no watcher Python process remains, remove the stale lock. Replace the path with the real archive path:
Remove-Item "D:\Rule34 Tag Archive\.r34-watcher\watcher.lock" -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Run run_now.bat. If it succeeds, re-enable the task:
Enable-ScheduledTask -TaskName "Rule34 Tag Watcher"
Do not casually delete the lock while a watcher is alive. Two concurrent writers are exactly what the lock is preventing.
Common failures
Missing authentication
Both credentials are required. Confirm user_id contains numbers only and api_key contains only the key value.
Unexpected API response type
Old builds hid string messages from the API. Current builds unwrap double-encoded JSON, treat “No images found” as an empty result, and display real API messages while redacting the configured API key.
Nothing downloads on the second normal run
That is usually correct. The first run establishes a baseline; later normal runs only download new discoveries. Use backfill for history.
The task exists but does not run after reboot
The task uses an interactive-logon principal. It runs while the configured Windows account is logged in. Check its action path with schtasks; if the project moved, reinstall the task.
The archive appears several times larger than the drive space used
Explorer is adding the logical size of every hard-link path. Check actual drive free space and verify links with fsutil hardlink list.
A tag file was deleted
The watcher repairs a missing managed link the next time that post is encountered. It does not redownload the bytes if the canonical file still exists.
Recovery scenarios
The project folder vanished, but the archive survived

Download the project again.
Create a new config.json pointing at the existing archive.
Use the same watched tags.
Run --check-config.
Run run_now.bat.
Reinstall the scheduled task.

The history database lives in the archive, so it should be found automatically.
The database vanished, but .r34-watcher\files survived
Make a backup first. Then run backfill. The watcher can recognize existing canonical files, rebuild records, and restore missing tag links without downloading those bytes again.
Everything vanished
Install from the repository, restore the tag lists and credentials, choose a new NTFS archive, test normally, and run backfill.
This is why the safe-to-share parts belong on GitHub and the secret config.json does not.
Running the test suite
From the project folder:
py -3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
The tests cover configuration validation, API response oddities, initial baselining, new-post checks, resumable multi-page backfill, General tags, one-download/multiple-link behavior, and link repair.
Reimplementing it from the design
If the source somehow disappears from every backup, these are the essential pieces:

Load and validate JSON configuration.
Represent every watched item as a category/tag pair.
Query the Rule34 DAPI with page=dapi, s=post, q=index, json=1, tags, pid, limit, user_id, and api_key.
Normalize normal lists, message strings, and double-encoded JSON responses.
Rate-limit and retry all requests.
Store tag initialization, per-tag post status, and canonical file paths in SQLite.
Download into a temporary .part file, verify it is non-empty, then atomically move it into the canonical store.
Use post ID plus file hash for collision-resistant filenames.
Use os.link to create every visible tag path from the canonical file.
Refuse to replace unrelated existing files.
Use a single-instance lock around database and archive changes.
Keep normal checks bounded; make full backfill explicit and resumable.
Log to both the console and rotating files.
Schedule only normal mode. Backfill remains a deliberate manual operation.

That is the whole machine.
One polite API client.
One memory.
One physical copy of every file.
As many useful folder paths as you want.
Good luck, Future Me.

projects/booru-image-downloader/guides/r.content:
Rule34 Tag Watcher 2.0
A small Windows downloader that checks Rule34.xxx for selected Copyright,
Character, Artist, and General tags. It uses the site’s JSON API,
keeps resumable SQLite history, and has no third-party Python dependencies.
One file, every matching folder
Version 2 stores each post’s bytes exactly once. If the same post matches a
watched character, artist, and general tag, it still appears as a normal file
inside all three folders, but those paths are NTFS hard links to one file.
They do not consume three copies of the image.
For example:
Rule34 Tag Archive\
├── Copyright\
│   └── example_series\
├── Character\
│   └── example_character\
├── Artist\
│   └── example_artist\
├── General\
│   └── example_general_tag\
└── .r34-watcher\
    ├── files\
    │   └── ...one canonical copy of each post...
    └── state.sqlite3
The files in the four category trees open, copy, rename, and browse like normal
files. Deleting one tag-folder link does not delete the underlying image while
another link still exists. Do not delete .r34-watcher: it contains the
canonical links and the history database.
Windows Explorer may add the apparent size of every visible link when showing a
folder’s Properties even though NTFS allocated the file only once. Drive free
space is the reliable measure of actual storage used.
Requirements

Windows 10 or 11
Python 3.10 or newer from python.org
An NTFS download drive or folder
A Rule34 numeric user ID and API key
A network connection while the watcher runs

Hard links cannot cross drives and are not supported by filesystems such as
exFAT or FAT32. The setup performs a real hard-link test before installing the
scheduled task. The canonical file and all category links are kept inside the
same selected archive root, so they remain on one volume.
Setup


Extract this entire folder somewhere permanent. Do not run it from inside
the ZIP or move the project folder after scheduling it.


Open PowerShell in the extracted folder.


Run:
powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\setup.ps1


Enter the download folder and exact site tag names. Separate multiple tags
in the same category with commas.


Enter only the numeric user ID and API key values. Do not include
user_id=, api_key=, &, or other URL fragments. API-key input is hidden.


Double-click run_now.bat to test the API and download the initial batch.


Setup creates config.json and installs a Windows Scheduled Task named
Rule34 Tag Watcher. The default schedule checks once per hour while your
Windows account is logged in.
The API key is stored as plain text in config.json because the unattended
task must read it. Keep the project folder private. The watcher redacts the key
from API error messages.
First run and scheduled checks

The first normal check downloads the newest 25 posts per tag by default and
records older scanned posts as a baseline.
Later scheduled checks download only newly discovered posts.
Each check scans up to three pages of 100 posts for every configured tag.
The same post is fetched from the network once and hard-linked into every
matching watched-tag folder.
JPEG, PNG, GIF, and WebP are enabled by default.
Failed downloads are not marked complete, so a later run retries them.
If a managed tag link is accidentally deleted, a later scan repairs it from
the canonical file without downloading the image again.

Downloading all historical posts
Double-click run_backfill.bat and confirm the prompt. It walks all available
API pages for all configured tags, including posts skipped by the initial
25-post baseline.

The scheduled task remains in new-post-only mode.
An interrupted backfill is safe to run again. It starts at the newest page,
skips completed entries, and continues toward older posts.
Overlapping posts across tags are downloaded once and receive additional hard
links instead of physical copies.
The one-second delay applies to API pages and files. Avoid reducing it; a full
history can take hours and the site may throttle abusive clients.
You may leave the scheduled task installed during backfill. A single-run lock
prevents both modes from running simultaneously.

To include historical videos, add .mp4 and .webm to the
downloads.allowed_extensions array in config.json before starting backfill.
Configuration reference

















































SettingPurposeoutput_directoryNTFS root folder for the archiveapi.user_idNumeric Rule34 user ID onlyapi.api_keyAPI key value onlywatched_tagsExact tags grouped by copyright, character, artist, and generalschedule.interval_minutesInterval used when installing the taskfirst_run_download_limit_per_tagInitial newest-post download countpages_per_checkNumber of API pages inspected during normal checksmax_downloads_per_tag_per_runSafety cap for one tag during a normal runallowed_extensionsFile types that may be savedsave_sidecar_metadataWhether to add JSON metadata beside each tag link
After changing schedule.interval_minutes, rerun install_task.ps1. Tag and
download settings take effect automatically on the next run.
Useful commands
Validate the configuration and test hard-link support without contacting the
site:
py -3 .\r34_tag_watcher.py --config .\config.json --check-config
Preview destinations without downloading:
py -3 .\r34_tag_watcher.py --config .\config.json --dry-run
Reinstall the task after changing its interval:
powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\install_task.ps1
Remove only the scheduled task:
powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\uninstall_task.ps1
Logs are stored in logs\watcher.log. Removing the task does not delete the
archive, configuration, logs, or history database.
Notes

Folder names are sanitized for Windows, but API searches use the exact tags
from config.json.
Filenames contain the post ID and file hash to prevent collisions.
Use the tool only for material you may lawfully access and retain, and follow
the site’s terms and rate limits.

I still can’t stop thinking about what could have been. Days later, and there’s still this yearning ache, like an echo in my soul.
I put the device away. It was making me feel conflicted. Regretful, even. There are some possibilities you probably shouldn’t get to hear.
And yet, despite my better judgment, I think I’m going to have to take it back out of its hiding place. Tune into another past that could have been.
The curiosity is becoming overwhelming.

I’m starting to understand the patterns a little better, but hearing the signal isn’t enough anymore. I need to see what it’s doing.
It felt like I pushed the radio about as far as it can go. So I added a television.
I expected it to help me observe the interference.
It did more than that, it opened up a whole new world of strange and interesting music.
I’m still trying to understand what I changed.

I went back.
Same song. Same experiment.
I wanted to know if what I heard was a fluke, or if the receiver would lead me somewhere else.
It did. There’s another version.
And somehow that makes the question of which one is “mine” even harder to answer…

projects/cosmic-raven-records/pinned-com.content:
004B - Pinned Comment
Watch on YouTube
Coming back to this after spending more time with the receiver. I think I was still making the wrong thing important.
I was obsessed with which version was better. Which one was mine. Whether borrowing from one of them counted as stealing.
I’m not saying those questions stopped mattering. But I went back through my notes from 004A and 004B.
The settings weren’t as identical as I thought.
One of the television controls was slightly off. Barely enough to notice. At the time I would have called that meaningless. I don’t anymore.
I’ve started learning that tiny changes can move the receiver much farther than they should.
So maybe I wasn’t choosing between two versions of the same song. Maybe I was looking at two completely different places.
I’m starting to think the dial is only part of the tuning.

projects/cosmic-raven-records/pinned-com.content:
005B - Pinned Comment
Watch on YouTube
Apparently “keep turning the dial” was more literal than I meant.
I decided to stop wandering for a night and try something repeatable instead: same source, same settings, same process, written down carefully enough that I could actually do it again.
It worked. Sort of.
I found a stable version and recorded it. Then I shut the receiver down, reset everything, and tried to return to the exact same place.
I got the song again.
It wasn’t the same recording.
I’m starting to think “same settings” does not mean “same place.”

Watch on YouTube
006B confirmed the part I was hoping I had just screwed up.
I reset the receiver and rebuilt everything from my notes. Same source, same settings, same process. The song came back, but 006A didn’t.
So I’m done treating the controls like coordinates. They seem to get me into the right neighborhood, but not to a specific address.
I’m running the experiment one more time before I touch anything.

projects/cosmic-raven-records/pinned-com.content:
006B - Pinned Comment
Third pass gave me the same answer.
Same source. Same settings. Same process. The song came back again, and once again it wasn’t the recording I had already found.
Three attempts. Three versions.
At this point I don’t think the receiver is failing to return me to the same place. I think I was wrong to assume there was only one place to return to.
I stopped after the third pass.
Mostly because I realized I had no reason to think the fourth would be the last.

projects/cosmic-raven-records/pinned-com.filePath: Projects/Cosmic Raven Records/Pinned Comments/006C - Pinned Comment.md
projects/cosmic-raven-records/pinned-com.title: 006C - Pinned Comment
projects/cosmic-raven-records/pinned-com.content:
006C - Pinned Comment
I never ran the fourth pass.
Instead I did the opposite.
I pulled the source out, dropped the Anchor to zero, and stopped trying to return to anything I already knew.
I’ve done that before, but somehow the receiver still found its way back to something familiar.
This time I deliberately pushed farther away.
That’s how I found 007A.
I don’t know the song.
I don’t know who made it.
As far as I can tell, I have never heard anything from them before.
That’s new.

projects/cosmic-raven-records/transmissi.content:
Cosmic Raven Records - Doomsday Rebuild Guide
If you are reading this because the original machine died, Windows was reinstalled, the Dropbox folder vanished, or Future Me has absolutely no memory of how any of this worked: hello.
This is how to rebuild the Cosmic Raven Records transmission-video workflow from scratch.
What this system actually does
You give one BAT file four things:
song file
transmission number
artist
track title
It uses FFmpeg to create:

a five-second acquisition intro,
the song beginning after that intro,
a 1920x1080 static-background transmission video with HUD text and an audio spectrum,
a 1280x720 YouTube thumbnail,
clean-ish filenames based on transmission / artist / title.

The current narrative descriptions are not generated by the BAT. Those live in the Google Doc Cosmic Raven Records - Transmission Script.

1. Rebuild the folder
Use something like:
Cosmic Raven Records\
├── make_transmission.v4.bat
├── assets\
│   ├── background_1.png
│   ├── intro_background_1.png
│   ├── intro.wav
│   ├── hud_overlay.png
│   ├── intro_overlay.png
│   └── thumbnail_overlay.png
├── output\
├── docs\
└── archive\
The production project used:
D:\Dropbox\[COSMIC RAVEN, LLC]\[RECORDS]
It does not have to live there, because the BAT works relative to its own location.

2. Install FFmpeg
On Windows, the original setup used the Gyan FFmpeg build installed through WinGet.
winget install Gyan.FFmpeg
Close and reopen the terminal, then verify:
ffmpeg -version
The workflow was built around FFmpeg 9.x, but it uses ordinary filters and should not require exactly that build forever.

3. Font requirement
The current BAT uses Windows Consolas:
C:\Windows\Fonts\consola.ttf
In the FFmpeg filter string the path appears as:
C\:/Windows/Fonts/consola.ttf
If that font disappears in a future Windows version, replace the FONT variable with another monospaced font path.

4. Restore the assets
The exact expected filenames are:
background_1.png
intro_background_1.png
intro.wav
hud_overlay.png
intro_overlay.png
thumbnail_overlay.png
Important: the raven logo is baked into the current overlays. Old prototypes used a separate logo.png; the current baseline does not.
If intro_background_1.png is missing, the script falls back to background_1.png.
All PNGs should be designed for a 1920x1080 canvas even though FFmpeg will scale them.

5. Run a test
Put a test WAV beside the BAT and run:
make_transmission.v4.bat "Test.wav" "999A" "Test Artist" "Test Track"
Expected output:
output\CRR_999A_Test_Artist_Test_Track.mp4
output\CRR_999A_Test_Artist_Test_Track_thumbnail.png
The exact filename sanitizer is intentionally simple in this baseline, so weird punctuation is worth testing before a real release.

6. How the audio works
The reliable version does not try to fake a five-second intro by merely delaying the song inside one complicated filter graph.
It first creates a temporary WAV:
0:00 - 0:05  assets\intro.wav
0:05 - end   selected song
That combined WAV becomes the final MP4 audio and also feeds the visualizer.
This solved earlier synchronization/introduction problems and is an important part of the known-good baseline.

7. Current video behavior
The main render is:
1920 x 1080
30 fps
H.264 / libx264
CRF 18
preset medium
yuv420p
AAC 320 kbps
The intro lasts five seconds.
After five seconds the main HUD appears with:
COSMIC RAVEN RECORDS
SIGNAL: LOCKED
TRANSMISSION ###
ARTIST
TRACK
ARCHIVE STATUS: STABLE
DIMENSIONAL NOISE: NORMAL
The current documented visualizer baseline is:
showfreqs
820 x 110
bar mode
log frequency scale
sqrt amplitude scale
cyan: 0x22D0E6
position: x=270, y=885
If the live production BAT differs, the live BAT wins. Update this guide after verifying it.

8. Thumbnail behavior
The thumbnail uses:
intro_background_1.png
thumbnail_overlay.png
and draws the transmission plus artist/title directly from the BAT arguments.
That direct-argument approach matters. An earlier version fed thumbnail labels through temporary text files and intermittently lost the text.
The thumbnail output is:
1280 x 720

9. Progress output
Do not go back to raw FFmpeg -stats unless you enjoy watching Windows Terminal vomit wrapping progress lines forever.
The working version uses:
-nostats
-progress pipe:1
and PowerShell converts the machine-readable progress stream into one updating console line.
FFmpeg errors are redirected to a temporary error file and displayed only when rendering fails.

10. Windows BAT landmines discovered the annoying way
Parentheses in filenames
Windows CMD can misparse filenames like:
Empty (Cover).wav
when variables are expanded inside parenthesized command blocks.
The safer pattern is labels + goto for validation/error handling.
FFmpeg drawtext colons
Literal colons inside drawtext need escaping:
SIGNAL\:
BAT continuation characters
A ^ must be the final character on its line. Trailing spaces after it can break the command.
Single PNG output
Use:
-frames:v 1 -update 1
Filter graphs
Do not try to use a simple -vf and a conflicting -filter_complex pipeline for the same output. Keep scaling/compositing inside the complex graph when needed.
Receiver timer
A %%{pts\:hms} receiver timer was tried and removed. Do not resurrect it unless there is a compelling reason.

11. Transmission numbering
The format is:
001A
002A
002B
003A
004A
004B
005B
006A
...
The number refers to an underlying song / signal / experiment.
The letter identifies a stable recovered version.
A and B are not proven coordinates. They are archive labels.
005A was deliberately skipped in the public archive. Do not “fix” the numbering.

12. Narrative source of truth
Use the Google Doc:
Cosmic Raven Records - Transmission Script
Do not maintain competing canonical description files unless they are clearly labeled snapshots.
Current project language:
A found-media music fiction project.
Longer description:
A transmedia fiction project built around music recovered from alternate realities.
Canonical slogan:
Music from somewhere else.

13. Disclosure block
Keep the fiction fun without trying to deceive anyone. The standard public disclosure is:
About Cosmic Raven Records:
This is a fictional music and worldbuilding project using a mix of human-created and AI-generated music, visuals, writing, direction, editing, and curation. The transmissions, artists, histories, and alternate realities are part of the fiction.
 
This is all an experiment.

14. If everything is gone
Recovery order:

Clone the Git repository.
Restore the live assets folder.
Install FFmpeg.
Verify Consolas or change the font path.
Run the 999A test render.
Restore/export the Google Doc narrative archive.
Compare output against an old YouTube transmission.
Only then start changing things.

If the original production assets are gone, use an old rendered transmission as the visual reference and rebuild new overlays at 1920x1080. The fiction does not require pixel-perfect preservation of the old HUD; the generator only requires the expected files to exist.

15. Future work, not rebuild requirements
Ideas already discussed but deliberately not required for recovery:

V4+ visual redesign
more animated backgrounds
better / layered visualizers
genre metadata
transmission classifications
Shorts templates
more interactive receiver visuals

Get the boring baseline working first. Then make it weird again.

projects/cosmic-raven-records/transmissi.content:
Cosmic Raven Records
Music from somewhere else.
Cosmic Raven Records is a found-media music fiction project: songs are presented as transmissions recovered through a fictional homemade receiver that appears to tune into alternate possibilities, timelines, or realities.
The public project mixes music, video, writing, worldbuilding, AI-assisted material, human-created material, editing, direction, and curation. The fiction never depends on pretending the project is literally real; the YouTube descriptions include a plain-language disclosure.
This repository exists for the very unglamorous reason that Future Me should not have to reverse-engineer Past Me’s batch file five years from now.
What is in here

make_transmission.v4.bat — Windows/FFmpeg transmission video + thumbnail generator.
assets/README.md — exact asset names the generator expects.
docs/Cosmic Raven Records - Doomsday Rebuild Guide.md — rebuild the workflow from a blank Windows machine.
docs/Transmission Generator - Technical Notes.md — how the render pipeline works and the important FFmpeg/CMD landmines.
docs/Story and Posting Guide.md — current narrative rules, transmission numbering, description structure, and pinned-comment strategy.
docs/Git Backup Setup.md — how to put the real working folder under Git/GitHub.
archive/README.md — what should be periodically snapshotted for long-term recovery.

Current generator usage
From the working directory:
make_transmission.v4.bat "Song.wav" "006A" "Artist Name" "Track Name"
Arguments are:

audio file
transmission number
artist
title

Outputs are written to output\ as an MP4 and a 1280x720 thumbnail.
Important
The BAT file in this repository was reconstructed from the last known working v3.9 baseline plus the v4 thumbnail-overlay change. Before replacing the copy on the production machine, compare it with the live file currently used in:
D:\Dropbox\[COSMIC RAVEN, LLC]\[RECORDS]
The current visual assets are not included in this bootstrap archive because the exact production copies were not available in the project files used to build this backup. Copy the live assets\ folder into the repository before treating the repo as a complete disaster-recovery backup.
Narrative source of truth
The working narrative/descriptions live in the Google Doc:
Cosmic Raven Records - Transmission Script
That document is the source of truth for posted descriptions and current drafts. Periodically export a Markdown or DOCX snapshot into archive\ so the story survives even if the live document disappears.

projects/cosmic-raven-records/transmissi.title: Story and Posting Guide
projects/cosmic-raven-records/transmissi.content:
Cosmic Raven Records - Story and Posting Guide
This is a practical continuity guide, not a rigid lore bible. The narrator is allowed to be wrong.
Core premise
The narrator accidentally built what he first called a radio. It does not seem to tune normal stations; it appears to tune possibilities.
He initially feeds old songs into it and receives alternate realized versions. Later he adds an old CRT television, which changes the behavior of the setup in ways that should not make sense. Eventually he begins finding music without feeding it a source at all.
Whether this is actually alternate realities, timelines, possibilities, some sort of generative machine, or something else should remain uncertain.
Machine vocabulary
These are narrator-invented terms, not proven physics.
Anchor — roughly how much of the source recording is being fed into the receiver. Stronger Anchor tends to keep the result closer to the source.
Drift — movement away from the source while tuning.
Depth — a harder-to-define behavior associated with the television controls; small changes can produce much more radical differences than simple performance variation.
Stability — how well a found signal holds together: static, CRT snow, breakup, and whether the controls can be released without losing it.
Device naming
Natural progression:
the radio
→ the radio and television
→ the setup
→ the receiver
Do not invent a grand official science-fiction device name unless the story earns it later.
Transmission IDs
TRANSMISSION 006A

number = underlying song / signal / experiment
letter = recovered stable version

Letters are archive labels, not coordinates.
The public archive intentionally jumps from 004B to 005B. Leave 005A unexplained.
Current narrator arc
The early narrator is frightened, compulsive, and ethically uncomfortable.
By 005B he stops treating curiosity as a moral failure and starts treating the receiver like a project.
The direction from here is:
fear → compulsion → guilt → surrender → fascination → competence → routine → gleeful obsession
The goal is not to make him generically insane. The impossible should gradually become mundane to him.
Serious and ridiculous music
Both belong.
The archive criterion eventually becomes less like:
Does this fit the serious tone?
and more like:
Did I find something worth preserving?
A haunting song and an absurd comedy song can sit next to each other because both are artifacts from the receiver.
Pinned comments
Pinned comments can function as later annotations.
The description represents what the narrator thought when the transmission was archived.
A later pinned comment can:

correct an earlier assumption
add a new machine observation
reinterpret old evidence
connect later discoveries backward
quietly seed future story ideas

Do not use every pinned comment as a teaser for the next upload.
Writing layout
For YouTube readability:

one paragraph = one idea
related short sentences stay in the same paragraph
blank lines mark real shifts in thought/time/subject
standalone one-line sentences are for emphasis, not default formatting
pinned comments are tighter than full transmission descriptions

Canonical public disclosure
About Cosmic Raven Records:
This is a fictional music and worldbuilding project using a mix of human-created and AI-generated music, visuals, writing, direction, editing, and curation. The transmissions, artists, histories, and alternate realities are part of the fiction.
 
This is all an experiment.
Useful labels for describing the project
Short:
A found-media music fiction project.
Longer:
A transmedia fiction project built around music recovered from alternate realities.

projects/cosmic-raven-records/transmissi.title: Transmission Generator - Technical Notes
projects/cosmic-raven-records/transmissi.content:
Transmission Generator - Technical Notes
This document is the quick technical reference for make_transmission.v4.bat.
Inputs
make_transmission.v4.bat "audio" "transmission" "artist" "title"
Example:
make_transmission.v4.bat "Empty (Cover).wav" "001A" "Nekroxx" "Empty"
Pipeline

Validate input audio and required assets.
Create a temporary 48 kHz / stereo PCM WAV containing five seconds of intro.wav followed by the source track.
Feed that combined WAV once as final audio and a second time into showfreqs for the visualizer.
Loop the static background and transparent overlay images for the duration of the audio.
Draw fixed HUD text plus temporary-file artist/title/transmission text.
Encode 1920x1080 H.264 video with AAC audio.
Create a separate 1280x720 thumbnail using the dedicated thumbnail overlay.
Delete scratch files.

Known baseline values
Intro: 5 seconds
Video: 1920x1080 @ 30 fps
Codec: libx264
CRF: 18
Preset: medium
Pixel format: yuv420p
Audio: AAC 320k
Visualizer: showfreqs 820x110
Visualizer color: 0x22D0E6
Visualizer position: 270:885
Font: Consolas
Scratch files
The generator may temporarily create:
.crr_transmission.txt
.crr_artist.txt
.crr_track.txt
.crr_credit.txt
.crr_ffmpeg_error.txt
.crr_audio_error.txt
.crr_combined_audio.wav
These should not survive a successful run.
Important provenance note
The archived make_transmission.v4.bat was reconstructed from the last known working v3.9 clean-intro-audio BAT plus the dedicated thumbnail_overlay.png V4 change.
It should be compared with the actual production BAT before being declared the final canonical copy.

I built a… ‘radio’. That’s the best thing to call it.
But it doesn’t seem to tune into places. It tunes into possibilities.
I know that sounds crazy, and I don’t know if I believe it myself yet, but I think I’m hearing what could have been. An alternate reality, I guess.
I gave it a song I wrote years ago-half finished, never fully realized. Like so many others. Something I knew well enough that I’d recognize it immediately.
I turned the dial.
Somewhere, somehow, somebody else was playing it.
This isn’t my version.
This is theirs.
Or maybe it’s the version that could have been.

projects/cosmic-raven-records/transmissi.content:
TRANSMISSION 002A [Shagwrath, Multi Theft Auto Theme [2]]
Watch on YouTube
I caved.
The allure of the unknown, and this morbid curiosity, won out over better judgment.
I keep telling myself that maybe this is a good thing. Maybe I made something extraordinary. Maybe I owe it to the world to share what I’m hearing.
But I can’t shake the feeling that this is dangerous.
All great technology can be dangerous in the wrong hands. But this feels different.
It feels like a drug.
I keep coming back to it.
I want more.
I’ve listened to alternate versions of songs I know. Old songs. New songs. Bands I grew up with. Things I thought I understood completely.
Sometimes the differences are obvious.
Sometimes they’re almost nothing.
A different choice in a melody. A vocal inflection. A guitar tone. A pause that lasts half a second longer.
And somehow those are the ones that get me the most.
I’ve spent dozens of hours turning the dials, trying to understand how this thing works. Trying to map it. Trying to find some pattern.
Maybe there is not one at all.
Maybe it’s just too complicated for me.
I’m just one man staring at something much bigger than I am.
I keep finding myself listening to multiple versions of the same song, trying to decide which one is better.
Worse than that, I catch myself wondering which one is closer to the version I would have made.
That thought bothers me more than I want to admit.
Maybe it’s better to distract myself with nostalgia.
Maybe I should be the martyr here. Keep the machine to myself. Keep everyone else safe from it.
Because I’m starting to wonder if the danger isn’t what the machine can show us.
Maybe the danger is how badly we want to keep looking.

projects/cosmic-raven-records/transmissi.content:
TRANSMISSION 003A [None, Unnamed]
Watch on YouTube
I think I’ve reached the limit of what I can do with the radio alone.
I’ve gotten better at finding signals. Or maybe I’ve just gotten better at recognizing what I’m looking for.
There’s one control I’ve started thinking of as the Anchor.
It’s really just the amount of the original recording I’m feeding into the radio, but the name seems appropriate. The stronger the source, the closer everything stays to what I remember.
Turn it down and things begin to… ‘drift’.
I’ve started writing down the positions of the dials. Frequencies. Input levels. Anything that might help me reproduce a result.
It helps.
Sometimes.
The problem is that hearing the signal isn’t enough anymore.
There are moments where I know something is there, buried underneath the static, but I can’t tell what I’m actually doing to it. I can turn the dial until the sound changes, but that doesn’t tell me why it changed.
So I added a television.
An old CRT. Nothing special.
The original idea was just to give myself something visual to look at while I was working. Feed the signal through it, watch the snow and interference move while I tuned the radio.
I thought maybe I could see patterns, some sort of visual indicator. Learn to recognize a good signal before I could hear it clearly.
That isn’t what happened.
The television must have changed the signal.
I don’t know how else to explain it.
Controls that should have absolutely nothing to do with the audio are affecting what comes through the radio.
Not just the quality of the reception.
The song itself.
I spent most of the night convincing myself I had wired something incorrectly, because I probably did.
But that doesn’t explain what I heard.
This transmission came from one of my old songs again.
At least, that’s where it started.
I’m beginning to think calling this thing a radio isn’t going to make sense for much longer, but I really don’t know what to call it anymore.

projects/cosmic-raven-records/transmissi.content:
TRANSMISSION 004A [Jedicide, The Seduction on the Darkside [1]]
Watch on YouTube
I tried to stay away.
I really did.
I had already wasted too much time listening to things that never happened. Songs I knew. Songs I didn’t. Familiar bands playing unfamiliar versions of familiar music.
And since adding the television, things have gotten stranger.
Some of what I’ve found is beautiful.
Some of it is… bizarre.
Some of it I genuinely don’t know what to make of, or if I can even call it music.
At some point I realized I was spending more time listening to what other versions of the world had made than actually making anything myself. That really bothered me.
So I decided to put it down for a while and to invest my energy into something productive. I went back through my old projects, old half finished songs and recording. Ideas from twenty years ago that never became what I thought they could be.
I started cleaning them up.
Rewriting things.
Finishing things.
Actually making music again instead of sitting in front of that machine lamenting and wasting time wondering what might have been.
It felt good.
i felt like I was doing better than ever.
Then the curiosity came back, and it grew stronger and stronger until I just couldn’t resist anymore.
Maybe I was right before.
Maybe this thing really is a drug.
Maybe it is dangerous.
I told myself I was only going to listen for a few minutes.
This time I didn’t feed it anything.
No recording.
No anchor.
I just started tuning.
And I heard something familiar.
It took me a few seconds to understand why.
It was the song I had been working on.
Not an old version.
Not something I had already recorded and forgotten.
The song I was working on now.
Except it was finished.
Fully realized.
And better.
At least, I thought it was better.
That should have been exciting.
Instead, it scared the hell out of me.
Because the more I listened, the more I realized something else.
It was closer to my version than these signals usually are.
Not identical.
But close.
And everything I had changed in my own song over the last few days seemed to be pushing it closer to what I was hearing through the receiver.
So which direction is this going?
Am I finding a version of the song that already exists somewhere else?
Or am I changing what I find by changing mine?
Was this always out there?
Did my work somehow pull me closer to it?
Or is the machine just showing me what I want to hear?
I don’t know which answer bothers me more.
And now I have another problem.
Because I heard things in that version that I want to use.
Ideas I never would have thought of.
Choices that make the song better.
But are they mine?
If another version of me wrote them, does that count?
Would taking them be inspiration?
Stealing?
Does it even matter if the person I’m stealing from is me?
I wanted this machine to show me what could have been.
I didn’t expect it to make me question what I’m allowed to make now.

projects/cosmic-raven-records/transmissi.title: 004B - Jedicide - The Seduction on the Darkside 2
projects/cosmic-raven-records/transmissi.content:
TRANSMISSION 004B [Jedicide, The Seduction on the Darkside [2]]
Watch on YouTube
I couldn’t leave it alone.
Not even for a few hours.
Damnit.
I’m right back where I started.
This thing I built is bad for me.
It’s all I can manage not to spend the entire day with it.
I kept thinking about that version of the song.
My song.
Was it really better?
Or did it only feel better because it was finished?
Because somebody else had already made all the decisions I was still struggling with?
Or was it simpler than that?
Maybe they were just the better composer.
I went back to the receiver.
Same song.
Same area of the dial.
As close as I could get to the settings from before.
And I found another one.
Not the same recording.
Not quite.
Some of the choices were different.
Things I liked in the first version were gone.
Things I hadn’t even noticed before had changed.
And there were new ideas.
Good ones.
Maybe better ones.
That was when I realized I had been asking the wrong question.
Looking at this from the wrong point of view.
There isn’t a better version.
There are just versions.
Different decisions.
Different circumstances.
Different people.
Or different versions of me.
I listened to both of them back to back.
Then I listened to mine.
Then theirs again.
Then mine.
Over and over.
At some point I stopped knowing what I actually preferred.
I started wondering which version I was supposed to prefer.
That scares me.
Because now I know I can keep turning the dial.
There could be ten more.
A hundred.
Maybe somewhere out there is a perfect version of this song.
Whatever that even means.
And if I find it, what am I supposed to do?
Copy it?
Learn from it?
Take the parts I like and pretend I would have gotten there eventually?
Ignore it and deliberately make something worse just so I can still call it mine?
If another version of me wrote it, does that make it mine too?
Or am I just stealing from someone because I know they can never stop me?
I wanted inspiration.
Instead I’ve given myself an infinite number of second guesses.
And worse than that, I’ve given myself a way to cheat.
I don’t know if that’s what this is.
But I don’t know what else to call it.
This thing…
I keep calling it a receiver.
Some days it feels more like a curse.

projects/cosmic-raven-records/transmissi.content:
TRANSMISSION 005B [Jedicide, The Rule of Two]
Watch on YouTube
I’ve been thinking about this all wrong.
For weeks I’ve treated the receiver like something I needed to resist. Something I should only touch for a few minutes before putting it away again.
That clearly isn’t working.
So I’m done pretending I don’t want to know what this thing can do.
I still don’t know if any of this is right. I’ve just stopped pretending that uncertainty is going to stop me.
I built an impossible machine.
Maybe it’s time I actually used it.
The radio and television are more or less permanently connected now. The workbench is a disaster. Wires everywhere. Notes taped to everything. Marks around the dials. Pages of settings that probably only make sense to me.
I’ve started giving the behaviors names.
Anchor.
Drift.
Depth.
Stability.
They aren’t technical terms. I don’t know enough to have technical terms. They’re just the words I keep writing in my notes because I needed some way to describe what I was seeing.
Anchor is the easiest.
It’s basically how much of the source I’m feeding into the receiver.
Drift is what I call the movement away from it.
Depth is harder.
The television gave me controls I didn’t have before, and tiny adjustments can push a signal somewhere completely different.
Not just a different performance.
Sometimes a different genre.
Different instruments.
Different lyrics.
Different everything.
Stability is the least mysterious. It’s just my shorthand for how well a signal holds together once I find it. How much snow is left on the screen. How much static is in the audio. Whether I can take my hands off the controls without losing it.
I’ve found things over the last few days that I don’t have words for yet.
Some of them are incredible.
Some of them are completely ridiculous.
And I’ve realized something.
I don’t need every signal to make sense.
I don’t need to decide which version is best.
I don’t even need to know what I’m looking for.
I just want to know what’s out there.
I can sit there for hours now, barely touching the controls, waiting for the static to change.
You start hearing patterns in it.
A rhythm buried underneath the noise.
A note that shouldn’t be there.
A voice for half a second.
Then you move the dial a fraction and suddenly there’s a whole song on the other side.
That still gets me.
Every single time.
There is so much out there.
More than I could ever listen to.
More than I could ever understand.
And for the first time since I built this thing, that thought doesn’t bother me.
It makes me want to keep turning the dial.

projects/cosmic-raven-records/transmissi.content:
TRANSMISSION 006A [Jedicide, Shadows of the Empire [1]]
Watch on YouTube
I wanted one clean experiment.
No wandering. No chasing a fragment just because something in the static caught my attention. Same source, same Anchor, same dial position, same television settings. I wrote everything down before I started.
The first pass was almost boring. The signal came in quickly. Stable picture. Clean audio. The song was right where I expected it to be.
I recorded it and thought, for once, maybe I was finally getting somewhere.
Then I shut the receiver down.
I reset everything, waited a while, and rebuilt the settings from my notes as carefully as I could.
I expected to find this recording again.
I didn’t.
I found the song. Same structure. Same identity. Close enough that I knew immediately I was in the right neighborhood.
But it wasn’t the same performance.
Different choices. Different details. Not dramatic, but unmistakable.
That should not happen if these controls are coordinates.
If I can put every knob back where it was and still arrive somewhere else, then either I’m missing a variable or the receiver does not work the way I’ve been assuming.
Maybe the settings don’t tell the receiver where to go.
Maybe they only tell it what kind of place to look for.
I don’t know yet.
So this is the first recording from the test.
I’m calling it 006A because I already know it isn’t alone.

TRANSMISSION 006B [Jedicide, Shadows of the Empire [2]]
Second pass.
I reset the receiver, rebuilt the settings from my notes, and checked everything twice before I started. Same source. Same Anchor. Same dial position. Same television settings.
The signal came back. The song came back.
006A did not.
This version is close enough that I’m not willing to call it random. Same structure. Same identity. Same neighborhood, if that’s the right word. But the performance is different again.
That rules out one of my assumptions. These controls aren’t coordinates. If they were, I should be able to return to 006A.
Maybe Anchor, Drift, and Depth don’t describe a location. Maybe they describe a range of possibilities the receiver can reach.
That leaves a more interesting question: once I’m inside that range, what determines which version I actually get?
I don’t know.
So I’m not changing anything yet. I’m going to reset it and do the exact same thing one more time.

TRANSMISSION 006C [Jedicide, Shadows of the Empire [3]]
Third pass.
I didn’t change anything.
Same source. Same Anchor. Same dial position. Same television settings. I rebuilt everything from the notes again and let the receiver settle.
The song came back.
So did another version of it.
That makes three.
At this point I’m comfortable saying the experiment worked. Just not in the way I expected.
The settings are repeatable. The result isn’t.
006A, 006B, and this one all occupy the same little neighborhood I’ve been tuning into, but they are not the same recording. Whatever the controls are doing, they seem to narrow the possibilities without selecting a single one.
That is useful.
It is also a little difficult to think about.
Because if I can reset the receiver and keep getting another valid version of the same song, I don’t know what would make that stop.
Maybe there are only a handful.
Maybe there are thousands.
Maybe asking how many is already the wrong question.
I almost reset it a fourth time.
Instead I wrote this down and walked away.
For now.

projects/cosmic-raven-records/transmissi.content:
TRANSMISSION 007A [Unknown, Untitled 1]
I finally stopped asking the receiver to show me something I already knew.
After 006, it felt like the obvious thing to try.
No source recording. Anchor at zero. Nothing for the receiver to follow back to me.
I’ve done that before, accidentally or otherwise, and it still managed to land on something familiar. So this time I kept moving.
More Drift than I usually allow. Small changes to the television. Let the picture roll. Let the audio disappear completely and then worked backward whenever something started pushing through the static.
For a while it was nothing.
Then there was a pulse.
A few notes. Drums underneath it. Something electronic, but heavier than most of what I’ve been finding.
I overshot it twice.
The third time I got the picture to hold long enough to bring the audio in clean.
And then I just sat there listening.
I kept waiting to recognize it.
A melody. A lyric. A riff. Anything that would connect it to something I’ve written, something I’ve heard, or one of the signals I’ve already recorded.
Nothing.
As far as I can tell, this has nothing to do with me.
That sounds obvious now that I’ve written it down, but it changes something.
Until tonight I could still tell myself the receiver was doing something to the material I gave it. Rearranging it. Extrapolating from it. Pulling possibilities out of things that were already there.
I don’t think I can use that explanation anymore.
There was no source.
There was just a song.
Someone made this.
Somewhere.
Or somewhen.
Or whatever word actually belongs here.
I don’t know who they are.
I don’t know where this came from.
I don’t even know if asking those questions the way I keep asking them makes sense.
But for the first time, I don’t think I found another version of one of my songs.
I think I found somebody else’s.
Holy shit.
I found somebody.

Dune Private Server Settings Reference
This is the configuration record for our self-hosted Dune: Awakening battlegroup immediately before the newly released build is audited.
It records:

settings Funcom deliberately exposed through the Battlegroup Editor or seeded UserSettings files;
additional settings we found in shipped defaults and tested ourselves;
the values currently used on our server;
the value types and ranges we can defend;
settings that looked promising but turned out to be cooked-asset, database-state, or runtime problems instead.

This is a known-good historical baseline, not a claim that every value survives the new build unchanged.

Scope rule: Funcom’s extracted DefaultGame.ini contains thousands of properties. Many are internal defaults, asset references, UI values, or untested class properties. This guide catalogs the administratively useful controls we exposed or investigated. A key merely existing in an extracted file does not make it a safe server setting.

Confidence labels





























LabelMeaningOfficial surfaceExposed by Funcom’s Battlegroup Editor or seeded self-host configuration.ConfirmedWe applied it and observed the expected behavior or persistence.Shipped keyPresent in shipped defaults, but our exact gameplay result still needs a controlled test.CandidateFound through asset/binary/database research; do not treat as a supported knob.Not a settingState or content that cannot be made persistent with a normal INI override.
What “acceptable values” means here
The server rarely publishes a formal minimum and maximum. This guide therefore separates:

formal range — explicitly documented in the shipped template;
type-safe range — the value shape the engine accepts, such as Boolean, integer, or finite float;
tested value — a value we actually used;
safe advice — a practical constraint intended to avoid pathological behavior.

If no formal range is known, the table says so. Do not mistake “parses successfully” for “balanced” or “safe.”

UserEngine.ini and UserGame.ini are global to the battlegroup. Use the Battlegroup Editor when different maps or partitions need different settings.

Database edits are not authoritative.Remove the altitude fuel penaltyNo safe scalar INI setting foundTreat as cooked gameplay data until a real override is proven.Increase only dynamic shipwreck encounter count/weightEncounter cadence is exposed, per-encounter weights/caps are notThe cadence settings increase broad random-encounter polling, not only wrecks.Directly tune CHOAM event count/weightAsset references were found, safe scalar controls were notAsset or runtime research required.Increase building-piece cap beyond the observed limitCandidate keys/assets exist, but no client/server-safe INI path was proven in our workDo not confuse landclaim segments or blueprint extensions with the piece cap.Increase the number of bases/sub-fiefs per playerNo confirmed INI keyLandclaim segment count is not the same thing as the per-player base/totem cap.
Known encounter assets found during research:

















MapAssetHagga BasinDA_DE_Tn_SmallShipWreck_01Deep DesertDA_DE_120_SmallShipWreck_DeepDesert_01
These asset names prove content exists; they are not numeric spawn settings.
Our live check found an active Hagga Basin shipwreck actor, BP_SmallShipwreck_01_C, but no evidence that more than one could be active concurrently. Faster encounter attempts did not override the encounter asset’s baked InstancesNumber or SpawnCooldown behavior.
Database/runtime state we successfully changed
These are useful discoveries, but they are not normal server settings.
Placed water cisterns
The stored amount is persisted in each cistern entity at:
FWaterStorageComponent → m_WaterStored
For our Medium Water Cisterns:

























FieldAccepted/tested valuem_WaterStoredInteger from 0 through 25000 per cisternCapacity used25000Cistern count16Filled total400000
The reliable workflow was:

Log the player out.
Stop Battlegroup completely.
Confirm no game-server pods are running and the database pod remains healthy.
Back up the database.
Update only the intended cistern entity rows.
Verify every changed row and commit.
Start Battlegroup normally.

Editing while the map server was running appeared to succeed in PostgreSQL, but the live process kept the old value in memory and overwrote the database on shutdown. Stopped-server timing was the difference between failure and success.
Inventory and storage capacity
dune.inventories.max_item_count and max_item_volume can be changed in PostgreSQL, but the game rebuilt our test container from its cooked template during startup. These columns therefore do not provide a persistent capacity setting for existing or newly built containers.
Syntax notes
Boolean spelling

Unreal object properties in UserGame.ini normally use True / False.
Console variables in UserEngine.ini may use 0 / 1 or lowercase true / false, depending on the key.
Preserve the spelling used in the known-good examples.

Arrays and maps

A leading + appends an Unreal array entry.
Repeating +m_PvpEnabledPartitions=... adds partition IDs.
Compound map values such as m_PerMapSystemSettings should be copied from the same build before editing.
Never replace a compound map with an isolated fragment unless the property is documented to merge rather than replace.

Client synchronization
At minimum, custom building-limit values such as m_MaxNumLandclaimSegments and m_bBuildingRestrictionLimitsEnabled may also need matching values in each player’s local client Game.ini. A mismatched client can show ghost placement behavior even when the server is authoritative.
Safe change procedure

Record the current game/server build.
Use 9. backup before risky changes.
Copy both UserEngine.ini and UserGame.ini somewhere safe.
Change one logical system at a time.
Restart with 3. restart.
Verify health with 1. status.
Check the actual gameplay behavior, not merely whether the file saved.
Record the test result and exact build in this guide.
Make a fresh backup after the server is healthy.

For database state changes, stop the relevant game process before writing unless that specific mutation has already been proven live-safe.
New-build audit checklist
When we begin the next deep dive:

 Record the new build/image number.
 Back up the database, Battlegroup spec, UserEngine.ini, and UserGame.ini.
 Diff the newly seeded configuration files against this baseline.
 Check whether the new build adds UserServerCustomSettings.ini or another official difficulty surface.
 Re-test every Confirmed setting after restart.
 Check for renamed sections, deprecated keys, and new formal ranges.
 Re-extract the complete m_PerMapSystemSettings value before restoring the 15/15 Hagga spice cap.
 Test whether the new difficulty controls expose storm intensity, item durability, base decay, XP, death-loot, survival, or Landsraad behavior.
 Revisit pause-on-empty/hibernation and base-power consumption.
 Revisit Deathstill timers, storage capacity, vehicle capacity, and the altitude fuel penalty.
 Revisit per-encounter shipwreck/CHOAM weights rather than only global encounter cadence.
 Check whether settings now replicate automatically to clients.
 Update each table’s shipped default, formal range, and validation status.

Provenance and further research
Primary operational source:

Funcom: Self Hosted Servers

Community extraction/research used to cross-check exact shipped keys:

snapetech/DuneAwakeningSelfHost — Server Config Keys
snapetech/DuneAwakeningSelfHost — Deep Desert Event Knobs
Icehunter/dune-awakening-truenas — Complete Server Settings

Our server’s confirmed values, failure modes, and database behavior come from our own tests. Community extractions are evidence of key names and shipped values, not a warranty that every key remains supported in later builds.
Change log
2026-09-26 — Initial paper baseline

Captured the known-good UserEngine.ini and UserGame.ini values.
Added encounter cadence, low-population Grandfather Worm, dew refresh, and Hagga spice-cap discoveries.
Separated official settings from shipped-but-untested properties.
Recorded asset/database dead ends so they are not rediscovered as fake INI solutions.
Added a focused checklist for auditing the newly released build.

projects/dune-awakening-private-server/g.content:
Dune Private Server Doomsday Guide
This is the “future me is tired, the server exploded, and I do not want to rediscover all of this again” guide.
The goal is to rebuild the Dune: Awakening self-hosted server from scratch on the dedicated Windows server, get the VM online, expose the correct ports, and avoid the specific traps that already ate multiple days of my life.
Known Working Server Context
Current dedicated server:
Host: ns518160.ip-158-69-52.net
Public IPv4: 158.69.52.183
OS: Windows Server 2022 Standard
RAM: 64 GB
Main NIC: Intel I350 Gigabit Network Connection / Onboard LAN 1
Gateway: 158.69.52.254
Steam app IDs:
Dune: Awakening main game: 1172710
Dune: Awakening self-hosted server tool: 4754530
Known working Dune server install path:
C:\PGN\DUNE
Known working SteamCMD path:
C:\PGN\STEAMCMD\steamcmd.exe
Avoid paths with brackets like:
C:\[PGN]\[DUNE]
PowerShell, SteamCMD, scripts, and wildcard handling can all become weird for no good reason. Use boring paths.
Big Picture Architecture
The working setup is:
Internet
  ↓
Windows Server public IP
  ↓
Windows Firewall
  ↓
Windows NAT
  ↓
Hyper-V Internal Switch
  ↓
Dune self-hosting VM
  ↓
Kubernetes / k3s
  ↓
Dune battlegroup pods
The important part is that the VM is not bridged directly to OVH’s public network.
That was a trap.
The working solution uses an internal Hyper-V switch and Windows NAT.
The Working Hyper-V / NAT Setup
Known working internal switch:
Bootyhole
Yes, that is the real name.
Known working VM IP:
192.168.69.69
Known working NAT subnet:
192.168.69.0/24
Known working NAT:
Bootyhole-NAT
The Dune VM should be connected to the Bootyhole internal switch.
Check Hyper-V Switches
On the Windows host, run PowerShell as Administrator:
Get-VMSwitch
Expected useful switch:
Name       SwitchType
----       ----------
Bootyhole  Internal
Check VM Adapter
Get-VMNetworkAdapter -VMName "dune-awakening" | Format-List *
Expected:
SwitchName: Bootyhole
IPAddresses: 192.168.69.69
Check NAT
Get-NetNat | Format-List *
Expected:
Name: Bootyhole-NAT
InternalIPInterfaceAddressPrefix: 192.168.69.0/24
Required Ports
Official/basic ports:
7777-7810 UDP  = game server player ports
31982 TCP      = RMQ
Also required in the known-good setup:
7888-7921 UDP  = IGW / inter-server gateway port range
That second UDP range matters. The server may appear in the browser and still fail to connect if this is missing.
Known Working NAT Port Forwards
On the Windows host, run PowerShell as Administrator.
UDP 7777-7810
for ($p = 7777; $p -le 7810; $p++) {
    Add-NetNatStaticMapping `
        -NatName "Bootyhole-NAT" `
        -Protocol UDP `
        -ExternalIPAddress "0.0.0.0" `
        -ExternalPort $p `
        -InternalIPAddress "192.168.69.69" `
        -InternalPort $p
}
UDP 7888-7921
for ($p = 7888; $p -le 7921; $p++) {
    Add-NetNatStaticMapping `
        -NatName "Bootyhole-NAT" `
        -Protocol UDP `
        -ExternalIPAddress "0.0.0.0" `
        -ExternalPort $p `
        -InternalIPAddress "192.168.69.69" `
        -InternalPort $p
}
TCP 31982
Add-NetNatStaticMapping `
    -NatName "Bootyhole-NAT" `
    -Protocol TCP `
    -ExternalIPAddress "0.0.0.0" `
    -ExternalPort 31982 `
    -InternalIPAddress "192.168.69.69" `
    -InternalPort 31982
Verify NAT Mappings
Get-NetNatStaticMapping |
    Where-Object {
        ($_.ExternalPort -ge 7777 -and $_.ExternalPort -le 7810) -or
        ($_.ExternalPort -ge 7888 -and $_.ExternalPort -le 7921) -or
        ($_.ExternalPort -eq 31982)
    } |
    Sort-Object ExternalPort |
    Format-Table NatName,Protocol,ExternalIPAddress,ExternalPort,InternalIPAddress,InternalPort
Windows Firewall Rules
Run PowerShell as Administrator.
New-NetFirewallRule `
    -DisplayName "Dune Awakening UDP 7777-7810" `
    -Direction Inbound `
    -Action Allow `
    -Protocol UDP `
    -LocalPort 7777-7810
 
New-NetFirewallRule `
    -DisplayName "Dune Awakening UDP 7888-7921" `
    -Direction Inbound `
    -Action Allow `
    -Protocol UDP `
    -LocalPort 7888-7921
 
New-NetFirewallRule `
    -DisplayName "Dune Awakening TCP 31982" `
    -Direction Inbound `
    -Action Allow `
    -Protocol TCP `
    -LocalPort 31982
Verify:
Get-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "Dune Awakening*" | Format-List *
Installing / Updating the Self-Hosted Server Tool
Use SteamCMD.
Example updater BAT:
@echo off
setlocal
 
set "STEAMCMD=C:\PGN\STEAMCMD\steamcmd.exe"
set "INSTALL_DIR=C:\PGN\DUNE"
 
"%STEAMCMD%" ^
  +force_install_dir "%INSTALL_DIR%" ^
  +login YOUR_REAL_STEAM_LOGIN_NAME ^
  +app_update 4754530 validate ^
  +quit
 
pause
Important:

Use the real Steam login name, not the display name.
Do not hardcode the password if you can avoid it.
If Steam Guard prompts, complete it.
The self-hosted server tool is app 4754530, not the main game app.

Starting the Battlegroup Tool
From Windows:
cd /d C:\PGN\DUNE
battlegroup.bat
Useful menu options we used:
1. status
2. start
3. restart
4. stop
5. update
6. edit
9. backup
13. open-file-browser
15. shell-vm
Exact menu names can change, but those numbers are what this install used.
First Setup
When the VM shell opens, it may say:
To start the setting up your own server type: setup and press the enter key
That is a generic login banner.
Do not rerun setup on a working server unless intentionally reconfiguring from scratch.
During initial setup only:
setup
You will need the Dune self-host token from the Dune account/self-host page.
Use SSH if possible instead of the Hyper-V console. Hyper-V console paste can inject garbage characters.
Known useful SSH command from Windows PowerShell:
ssh dune@192.168.69.69
UserSettings Files
Open with:
battlegroup.bat → 13. open-file-browser → UserSettings
There are two main files:
UserEngine.ini
UserGame.ini
Settings in these files apply to every server in the battlegroup.
If different maps/partitions need different settings, use the battlegroup editor instead.
Known Good UserEngine.ini Shape
; Settings in these config files will be applied to every server in the battlegroup
; If you need to override different settings for different servers, use the battlegroup editor instead
 
[URL]
Port=7777
IGWPort=7888
 
[ConsoleVariables]
Bgd.ServerDisplayName="YOUR SERVER NAME"
Bgd.ServerLoginPassword="YOUR PASSWORD"
 
Dune.GlobalMiningOutputMultiplier=2.0
Dune.GlobalVehicleMiningOutputMultiplier=2.0
SecurityZones.PvpResourceMultiplier=5.0
 
dw.VehicleDurabilityDamageMultiplier=1.0
 
Sandstorm.Enabled=1
Sandstorm.Treasure.Enabled=1
 
sandworm.dune.Enabled=1
Vehicle.SandwormCollisionInteraction=false
Sandworm.SandwormDangerZonesEnabled=true
Vehicle.SandwormInvulnerabilitySecondsOnExit=900.0
Vehicle.SandwormInvulnerabilitySecondsOnServerRestart=7200.0
Known Good UserGame.ini Shape
; Settings in these config files will be applied to every server in the battlegroup
; If you need to override different settings for different servers, use the battlegroup editor instead
 
[/Script/DuneSandbox.PvpPveSettings]
m_bShouldForceEnablePvpOnAllPartitions=False
;+m_PvpEnabledPartitions=1
;+m_PvpEnabledPartitions=2
 
[/Script/DuneSandbox.SecurityZonesSubsystem]
m_bAreSecurityZonesEnabled=True
 
[/DeteriorationSystem.ItemDeteriorationConstants]
UpdateRateInSeconds=1.0
 
[/Script/DuneSandbox.SandStormConfig]
m_bCoriolisAutoSpawnEnabled=False
 
[/Script/DuneSandbox.BuildingSettings]
m_MaxNumLandclaimSegments=12
m_BuildingBlueprintMaxExtensions=8
m_BaseBackupMaxExtensions=16
m_bBuildingRestrictionLimitsEnabled=True
Applying Config Changes
After editing UserEngine.ini or UserGame.ini:
3. restart
1. status
Do not reboot the entire Windows server unless you need to.
Backups
Before scary operations:
9. backup
Do this before:

deleting battlegroups
restoring backups
major updates
risky config changes
anything involving database/state

After the server is healthy again, make a fresh backup.
Kubernetes Commands
Open shell:
battlegroup.bat → 15. shell-vm
List namespaces:
sudo kubectl get namespaces | grep funcom
Real current battlegroup namespace:
funcom-seabass-sh-238803c537a22e2-fdofyf
Old deleted/bad unused battlegroup:
funcom-seabass-sh-238803c537a22e2-krmfhh
List pods:
sudo kubectl -n funcom-seabass-sh-238803c537a22e2-fdofyf get pods -o wide
Events:
sudo kubectl -n funcom-seabass-sh-238803c537a22e2-fdofyf get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -40
Describe a pod:
sudo kubectl -n funcom-seabass-sh-238803c537a22e2-fdofyf describe pod POD_NAME
Previous crash logs:
sudo kubectl -n funcom-seabass-sh-238803c537a22e2-fdofyf logs POD_NAME --previous --tail=160
Known Problem: Special Area Fails to Load
Symptom:

A special area / DLC area will not load
Status shows a map stuck in startup
Pod describe shows OOMKilled
Exit code 137
Memory limit is too low, often 5Gi

Example fix:
battlegroup.bat → 6. edit
Find the affected map/server and increase memory.
Example:
5Gi → 8Gi
or:
5Gi → 10Gi
Then:
3. restart
1. status
If the pod stops getting OOMKilled and becomes ready, that was the issue.
Known Problem: Server Visible But Cannot Connect
Check these first:
Get-NetNatStaticMapping |
  Where-Object {
    ($_.ExternalPort -ge 7777 -and $_.ExternalPort -le 7810) -or
    ($_.ExternalPort -ge 7888 -and $_.ExternalPort -le 7921) -or
    ($_.ExternalPort -eq 31982)
  } |
  Sort-Object ExternalPort |
  Format-Table NatName, Protocol, ExternalIPAddress, ExternalPort, InternalIPAddress, InternalPort
Make sure both UDP ranges exist:
7777-7810 UDP
7888-7921 UDP
Also check firewall rules.
The 7888-7921 UDP range was likely the missing piece during the first successful connection.
Known Problem: Blank Game Server Rows / CrashLoopBackOff
Symptom:
Database/Gateway/Director healthy
Game server rows blank
Server not visible or not usable
Pods show CrashLoopBackOff
Check pods:
sudo kubectl -n funcom-seabass-sh-238803c537a22e2-fdofyf get pods -o wide
If Overmap / Survival are crashlooping:
sudo kubectl -n funcom-seabass-sh-238803c537a22e2-fdofyf logs POD_NAME --previous --tail=160
Known Problem: Bad Funcom Build
This actually happened.
Symptoms:

Server was working previously
Later no server appeared correctly in browser
Restart did not fix it
Update initially re-applied the same bad build
Infrastructure healthy
Overmap and Survival crashloop
Exit code 139
SIGSEGV / segmentation fault
Fatal log references missing Spice data table

Crash clue:
Failed to load data table property 'm_SpiceFieldTypeDataTable'
/Game/Dune/Systems/SpiceHarvesting/DT_SpiceFieldTypes
Local checks that did not fix it:
sudo grep -R --line-number -E "DT_SpiceFieldTypes|m_SpiceFieldTypeDataTable|SpiceHarvesting" /home/dune /funcom 2>/dev/null | head -200
No result.
sudo find /funcom /home/dune -iname "*SpiceField*" -o -iname "*DT_Spice*" 2>/dev/null | head -100
No result.
Disk was fine:
df -h
Image reimport did not fix it:
sudo k3s ctr -n k8s.io images rm registry.funcom.com/funcom/self-hosting/seabass-server:2007976-0-shipping
Then update/restart still failed.
Conclusion:
Funcom pushed a bad build.
Actual fix:
Wait for Funcom to publish a fixed build.
Run battlegroup update.
Restart battlegroup.
Check status.
Checking Loaded Images
sudo k3s ctr -n k8s.io images ls | grep seabass-server
Useful when trying to confirm which build is loaded.
Bad build seen during incident:
2007976-0-shipping
Older images may remain locally. Do not manually force old builds unless there is no safer rollback path.
Deleting an Unused Battlegroup
Only do this after confirming:

real battlegroup is healthy
backup exists
the target namespace has no useful resources
the target battlegroup is definitely not your world

Known real battlegroup:
sh-238803c537a22e2-fdofyf
Deleted unused battlegroup:
sh-238803c537a22e2-krmfhh
Check namespaces:
sudo kubectl get namespaces | grep funcom
Check unused one:
sudo kubectl -n funcom-seabass-sh-238803c537a22e2-krmfhh get all
If it says:
No resources found
Delete namespace:
sudo kubectl delete namespace funcom-seabass-sh-238803c537a22e2-krmfhh
Verify:
sudo kubectl get namespaces | grep funcom
Expected:
funcom-operators
funcom-seabass-sh-238803c537a22e2-fdofyf
Things Not To Do Casually
Do not casually delete:
funcom-seabass-sh-238803c537a22e2-fdofyf
That is the real world.
Do not rerun:
setup
on a working VM unless intentionally rebuilding.
Do not wipe namespaces without backup.
Do not assume a blank status screen means networking. It may be Kubernetes/game server crashlooping.
Do not assume every crash is memory. Check exit codes and logs.
Quick Health Checklist
After updates or restarts:
1. status
Look for:
DB healthy
Gateway healthy
Director healthy
Game servers populated
Overmap running/ready
Survival_1 running/ready
No CrashLoopBackOff
No blank map names
From shell:
sudo kubectl -n funcom-seabass-sh-238803c537a22e2-fdofyf get pods -o wide
Bad signs:
CrashLoopBackOff
OOMKilled
Exit Code 139
Exit Code 137
serverReady: false
blank partitionMap/serverGuid annotations
Emergency Summary
If rebuilding from scratch:

Install SteamCMD.
Install app 4754530 to C:\PGN\DUNE.
Enable Hyper-V.
Use internal switch, not OVH bridged networking.
Recreate Bootyhole internal switch and NAT.
Give VM 192.168.69.69.
Forward UDP 7777-7810.
Forward UDP 7888-7921.
Forward TCP 31982.
Open same ports in Windows Firewall.
Run battlegroup.bat.
Complete setup once with token.
Configure server name/password/settings.
Start battlegroup.
Check status.
Test browser visibility.
Test actual connection.
Make a backup.

Final Note
The funniest part of this entire setup is that once it works, it works really well.
The least funny part is that every layer can lie to you.
The server can be installed correctly.
The VM can be running.
The database can be healthy.
The gateway can be healthy.
The server can even show in the browser.
And then one missing UDP range, one low memory limit, or one bad Funcom build can make it look haunted.
So check the layers one at a time.
Do not panic.
Do not delete the real namespace.
And absolutely preserve the Bootyhole switch unless there is a very good reason not to.

Garth’s Game DMG
Garth’s Game I is an actual Game Boy virtual-pet game built in C with GBDK 2020.
Garth has persistent needs, moods, minigames, dialogue, a synthesized voice, music, sound effects, SRAM saving, and progression. The current playable build has three care stats and three minigames. The next version is a major visual/gameplay redesign with a new home screen, a fourth GAS stat, four named minigames, jokes, and mood-driven animation.
The ultimate goal is not only a ROM.
I want a cartridge, label, box, and manual.
Current state

Sound effects

Stat-cap progression from 30 toward 100
Four randomized menu backgrounds

Redesign in progress

New cabin home screen
Animated Garth based on mood
FOOD, FUN, POWER, and inverse-pressure GAS
Four consistent title/game/results minigames
