updates/2026-09-21---star-wars-battlefro.title: 2026-09-21 - Star Wars Battlefront II Server Development
updates/2026-09-21---star-wars-battlefro.content:
I Accidentally Built Modern Infrastructure For A 2005 Star Wars Game
This started because I wanted to run a Battlefront II server.
The 2005 one. You know, the good one.
I have been running game servers for PGN for years, so the basic idea did not seem especially complicated.
Install the game.
Pick some maps.
Give the server a stupid name.
Play Battlefront.
Classic PGN Style.
So I brought PGN - Ewok Around and Find Out online.
It is a private (for now) STAR WARS Battlefront II Classic server running the GOG server build through SWBF2Admin on a Windows dedicated server.
Conquest only.
No heroes. (usually)
No friendly fire.
Just twenty-year-old Star Wars men shooting each other over command posts like God intended.
Naturally, this became an infrastructure project.
The first problem was simply keeping the damn thing online.
Battlefront II is old enough to drink, and the software around its dedicated server is from a very different era of Windows administration.
The server would run.
It would appear in the public server list.
Steam players could join the GOG-hosted server.
Then sometimes it would disappear even though the process still looked alive.
For a while I thought closing the remote desktop window was killing it.
That turned into a long series of tests involving Chrome Remote Desktop, Windows Remote Desktop, GOG Galaxy, SWBF2Admin, automatic restarts, RCON timeouts, and me repeatedly asking:

Okay, but is it actually still in the list?

Eventually I confirmed that the server could remain public and joinable for almost twenty-four hours through a Chrome Remote Desktop console session.
I also found the warning in SWBF2Admin’s own documentation: standard Windows Remote Desktop can interfere with the GOG server’s communications and make it disappear from the public master list.
That is an incredibly specific problem.
It is also exactly the kind of problem you get when you build modern infrastructure around a game released in 2005.
Chrome Remote Desktop is currently the known-good workaround. I do not love that. In fact, let me be honest. I loathe it… with hate.
So let’s ignore that for now.
Denial is not just a river in Africa.
Once the server itself was reasonably stable, I started digging into SWBF2Admin.
It provides a local WebAdmin dashboard, match management, player administration, statistics, announcements, and a Lua command system.
Lua, you say?
I claimed my in-game administrator account and started experimenting.
The first useful custom command was not useful at all:
!ping
It replied:
PONG! SWBF2Admin Lua is working.
That tiny stupid command was important because it proved the whole path worked.
The game could see a command.
SWBF2Admin could execute custom Lua.
Permissions worked.
The response made it back into the game.
I also tried using Lua to lock human players onto one team for future PvE ideas.
That did absolutely nothing. Then I tried more and more. That also did not work. Anyone for a nice African river cruise?
Both versions of the experiment failed, which at least told me that team locking will probably require server-side mission work instead of one magic function call.
Not every experiment needs to become a feature.
Sometimes the result is just:

Well, that is not how that works.

Then I found the statistics system.
SWBF2Admin was already capable of recording completed matches, player performance, kills, deaths, points, and map history into a SQLite database.
The information was there, to my surprise and delight.
It was just hiding behind right-clicking a completed match and opening its Details window like a secret menu in a restaurant.
Once I knew the data existed, the obvious next thought was:

I should put this on a website.

I first built a basic PHP Top 10 leaderboard.
Then I rebuilt the whole thing as a SvelteKit and Tailwind landing page served through the existing XAMPP/Apache setup on helvete.pizza.
The website reads the SWBF2Admin database locally and exposes the useful community-facing information without publishing the database itself.
It has a proper server landing page, a Season 1 leaderboard (Bryce’s idea), and a foundation for archived seasons later.
Season 1 currently includes all recorded matches because there was no reason to invent a preseason that nobody knew existed.
That felt like enough.
It was not enough.
I wanted the game server and Discord to talk to each other. There were naysayers. Why? Is that it is cool not enough? Fine. Ou la laa you can enter commands between Discord and the game server and, yes, talk. To nay sayers I say nay.
So I built a Node.js bridge and named the bot HK-47.
QUERY: Why would I not?
HK-47 connects to the local WebAdmin interface and bridges chat between Battlefront II and the PGN Discord server.
Messages sent in #swbfii-chat appear in the game.
Messages from players in the game appear in Discord.
System messages and commands are filtered out so Discord does not become a firehose of internal server garbage.
Discord formatting is neutralized before game messages are sent back out.
Messages are bounded, forced onto one line, and prevented from becoming accidental admin commands.
The first version had the usual collection of dumb integration problems.
Discord said Missing Access because I had authorized an application but had not actually installed the bot correctly.
WebAdmin returned HTTP 400 because it wanted localhost instead of 127.0.0.1.
Those are technically different addresses if you are a twenty-year-old game administration tool with strong opinions.
Once two-way chat worked, I added map awareness.
SWBF2Admin knows the maps by codes like:
dea1c
tat2c
cor1c
Those are useful to the server.
They are not especially useful to a normal human being who wants to know what map is next.
So HK-47 learned the actual map, era, and mode names, with support for both the stock maps and friendly names supplied by WebAdmin for custom maps.
I made a test command:
!battle
It worked! It gets a readable current and next battle message instead of raw internal codes.
Then I made HK-47 announce the battle automatically.
It announces after it detects the first active match, announces again when the current or next map changes, and repeats the status every sixteen minutes without spamming the same message constantly.
The bridge has fifteen automated tests covering chat handling, commands, map labels, announcement timing, authentication, WebAdmin parsing, message safety, and the client session itself.
All fifteen pass.
That was the point where this stopped feeling like a weird batch file attached to an old game and started feeling like a real little service.
Which led directly to the next question:

What happens when the dedicated server explodes?

At that point the project existed in too many places.
There was the live game installation.
There was SWBF2Admin and all of its XML, Lua, server settings, and database files.
There was the Discord bridge source and its secret environment file.
There was the editable SvelteKit website.
There was the compiled website actually being served by Apache.
There were a bunch of things I knew because I had just spent days figuring them out, which is another way of saying they were about to be forgotten forever.
So I built a proper disaster-recovery system.
The first half is a sanitized GitHub repository.
I wrote a PowerShell exporter that copies the safe, irreplaceable parts of the live server into a clean repository structure:
discord-bridge
swbf2admin-config
website/source
website/live-deployment
scripts
It preserves the bridge source and tests, SWBF2Admin configuration, Lua commands, server rotation, editable website, exact live website deployment, and recovery scripts.
It also sanitizes known password fields and refuses to include things that absolutely do not belong in Git:
.env
SQLite databases
logs
executables
DLLs
game assets
passwords
tokens
I tested the exported bridge source.
Fifteen tests passed.
I copied the website source into a completely separate temporary folder, installed it from the package lock, ran the Svelte checks, and built a fresh production deployment.
Zero errors.
Zero warnings.
Successful build.
Then I pushed the whole safe recovery snapshot to GitHub.
That protects the code and configuration, but it deliberately does not protect the most sensitive state.
The player statistics database cannot go in GitHub.
The Discord token cannot go in GitHub.
The live WebAdmin and server passwords cannot go in GitHub.
Unfortunately, those are also the exact things I would need after a catastrophic failure.
So the second half is a private encrypted backup.
I wrote another PowerShell script that refuses to run while Battlefront II or SWBF2Admin is active, because copying a live SQLite database and hoping for the best is how you create a backup that becomes exciting only when you desperately need it.
The script collects the database, Discord bridge environment, unsanitized private configuration, server rotation, and a recovery manifest containing the matching Git commit.
Then it creates a 7-Zip archive with AES-256 encryption, including encrypted filenames.
It tests the archive.
It generates a SHA-256 checksum.
It removes the temporary plaintext staging folder.
If anything fails, it removes the incomplete archive instead of leaving behind something that merely looks like a backup.
Naturally, the first version found an exciting PowerShell edge case where a one-item process list stopped behaving like a list.
That is fixed now.
I also did not want the only private backup sitting on the same dedicated server it was supposed to protect.
That would be less like disaster recovery and more like placing a spare key inside the burning house.
So I created a restricted Dropbox app folder and configured rclone on the dedicated server.
The server can access only its own backup area inside Dropbox.
It cannot browse the rest of my account.
An hourly Windows Scheduled Task runs as SYSTEM, looks for new encrypted archives, verifies their local checksums, uploads them, retries temporary failures, and confirms the remote files exist with matching sizes.
It never overwrites a conflicting backup.
It never deletes a local backup.
It never deletes a Dropbox backup.
My home computer then receives the off-server copy through the normal Dropbox client.
We created a real backup and watched both the encrypted archive and its checksum arrive.
Hell yes.
I also wrote the doomsday documentation.
There is now a complete recovery README covering the folder layout, installation order, server settings, bridge setup, website deployment, secrets, validation, known landmines, and how to rebuild the entire stack from a blank Windows server.
The wider project is documented as an Obsidian wiki too.
It has pages for architecture, normal operation, Discord, SWBF2Admin, the website, statistics, recovery, security, experiments, failed approaches, research, current status, decisions, and the development roadmap.
Because I know exactly what Future Me would do without that documentation.
He would open the server, stare at six vaguely related folders, and say:

What the fuck did I do here?

Now he has instructions.
You are welcome, asshole.
So that is the PGN Battlefront II server now.
A public server for a 2005 game.
A WebAdmin stack.
A persistent statistics database.
A seasonal leaderboard.
A custom two-way Discord bridge named after a homicidal protocol droid.
A tested source repository.
An encrypted off-site backup system.
And enough documentation to resurrect the whole thing after a small meteor strike.
The next job is to eliminate Chrome Remote Desktop.
That does not mean blindly switching to normal Windows Remote Desktop, because that is the thing most strongly associated with the server disappearing from the public list.
I need a remote-control setup that preserves the real console session, survives a reboot, lets me manage the server safely from home, and does not disturb GOG or SWBF2Admin.
Chrome Remote Desktop will remain installed as the emergency fallback until the replacement has proven all of that.
After remote access is settled, the roadmap moves into the fun community systems: persistent PGN player identity, profiles, lifetime statistics, XP, levels, ranks, nicknames, awards, achievements, credits, and eventually increasingly questionable ideas involving gambling and a persistent campaign.
That will be another post.
For now, the important part is that the server works, the community layer works, the source is protected, and the private state exists somewhere other than the machine that could die.
Not bad for wanting to play an old Star Wars game.
PGN Star Wars Battlefront II Dedicated Server Disaster Recovery

updates/2026-09-22---i-made-a-discord-ac.title: 2026-09-22 - I Made A Discord Activity and Accidentally Built An API!
updates/2026-09-22---i-made-a-discord-ac.content:
I Made A Discord Activity And Accidentally Built An API
This started because I wanted to remake a stupid little game.
Safe Cracker is simple.
There is one safe every day.
It has a four-digit combination from:
0000-9999
You guess a number.
The game tells you:
HIGHER
or:
LOWER
and you keep going until you crack it.
That is basically the whole game.
No complicated inventory.
No skill tree.
No twelve-hour tutorial.
No battle pass featuring Tactical Safe Pants.
Just you, a number, and the rapidly increasing realization that you absolutely should have remembered whether 4200 was too high.
The scoring is equally simple.
Fewest guesses wins.
If two people use the same number of guesses, fastest time wins.
I had made versions of this idea before, but this time I wanted it to live inside Discord as an Activity.
That seemed reasonable.
Make a little web game.
Put it in Discord.
Done.
Naturally, I built an authentication system, an API, a database, a leaderboard service, production infrastructure, HTTPS certificates, persistent sessions, Rich Presence, and a social sharing system.
This happens to me a lot.
The game itself came first.
I built it with SvelteKit and TypeScript.
The first version was intentionally ugly.
I did not want to spend three days making glowing buttons before I knew if the game actually felt good.
The important part was making the guessing loop fast.
You enter a four-digit number.
Hit Enter.
Immediately start entering another guess.
The game never waits for an animation.
It never locks the keypad while HIGHER or LOWER is displayed.
It never makes you watch some cute little transition before accepting another number.
Safe Cracker does not wait for the player.
The feedback flashes briefly and disappears.
That matters more than it sounds.
A huge part of the game is remembering the range in your own head while trying to move quickly.
If the game kept a visible guess history or showed the current minimum and maximum values, it would basically solve half the puzzle for you.
So it does not.
You have to remember.
Skill issue.
Once the prototype felt right, I needed an actual daily safe.
The game uses Central Time as the authoritative clock because that is where I am and apparently I have appointed myself the International Commissioner of Safe Time.
Every calendar day maps to a Safe number.
The launch date is Safe #001.
The next day is Safe #002.
And so on.
The combination itself is generated deterministically on the server using HMAC-SHA256 and a private secret.
That means the same date always produces the same safe combination without me having to manually create thousands of daily puzzles.
It also means the answer never needs to exist in the browser before the player solves it.
The client knows:
Safe #009
The server knows:
Nice try.
That distinction became increasingly important because I decided the server should be authoritative about basically everything that matters.
The browser does not decide how many guesses you made.
The browser does not decide your final time.
The browser does not decide whether you already completed today’s safe.
The server does.
The first guess creates the run.
Every valid guess increments the attempt count in SQLite.
The first guess starts the official timer.
The correct guess stops it.
If you close Discord halfway through and come back later, your run is still there.
I tested that specifically.
I made a few guesses, closed the Activity, waited, reopened it, and watched the timer jump forward correctly.
The safe had not forgotten me.
Unfortunately.
Once a run has started, you are committed.
Closing the Activity does not magically stop time.
Once you crack the safe, you cannot replay it that day for a better score.
That would make the leaderboard fairly pointless.
This was also around the time I realized:

Oh shit. I am making an API.

That was genuinely exciting.
“Make an API” has been one of those vague programming bucket-list things in my head for years.
Apparently I just needed to stop thinking about APIs and start trying to make a tiny safe game.
Safe Cracker now has several actual HTTP endpoints:
GET  /api/daily
POST /api/token
GET  /api/me
GET  /api/run
POST /api/guess
GET  /api/stats
GET  /api/health
The Svelte frontend talks to those endpoints.
Some are public.
Others require an authenticated session.
The browser sends guesses to the server.
The server checks the answer, records the attempt, calculates the official elapsed time, and sends back the result.
That is an API.
Look at me go.
Naturally, none of this was useful inside Discord until I knew who the player actually was.
So I wired in Discord OAuth through the Embedded App SDK.
When Safe Cracker launches inside Discord, it asks Discord to identify the player.
The authorization code goes to my server.
The server exchanges it with Discord.
Then the server independently asks Discord who that token belongs to instead of simply trusting whatever identity the browser claims it has.
The player gets stored in SQLite.
Then Safe Cracker creates its own random session token, stores only the hash in the database, and gives the browser an HttpOnly Secure cookie.
So Discord authenticates who you are.
Safe Cracker maintains its own authenticated session afterward.
That sentence makes this project sound approximately nine hundred times more sophisticated than:

Guess the number, idiot.

But here we are.
There was, of course, an authentication bug.
I had added logic that removed old Safe Cracker sessions whenever a new one was created.
That part worked.
Unfortunately, while editing the function, I removed the part where it actually returned the new session token.
So the login process successfully created a session and then immediately attempted to read:
session.token
from:
undefined
Beautiful.
The Activity responded with the highly informative message:
Discord auth failed
After digging through the actual code, I found the missing:
return {
    token,
    expiresAt
};
and everything came back to life.
That bug also taught me something useful about the build process.
npm run build
can successfully build the application without catching every TypeScript mistake.
So now the ritual is:
npm run check
npm run build
Much better.
Once accounts and daily runs were persistent, the next obvious feature was competition.
I added streaks.
Current streak.
Best streak.
Total safes cracked.
The current streak has one rule I particularly like:
Your streak does not die merely because you have not played today’s safe yet.
If you completed yesterday, your streak remains alive throughout today.
It only breaks once an entire day has actually been missed.
That sounds obvious, but “obvious” things still have to become actual database logic.
Then came the daily leaderboard.
Players are ranked by:
1. Fewest guesses
2. Fastest time
3. Completion time as a stable final tiebreaker
The game returns the Top 10 and also returns your own rank separately if you are outside the Top 10.
The first leaderboard was not especially competitive.
It was me.
Rank #1.
Also last place.
An incredible performance.
I tested the whole persistence chain by completing Safe #001.
The result was:
22 guesses
03:00.55
Then I closed the Activity.
Reopened it.
Same result.
Same completed state.
Same leaderboard entry.
No replay.
That was the moment the backend stopped feeling theoretical.
The little game had memory.
Then I needed somewhere for the thing to actually live.
I already run a Windows server with XAMPP and Apache for helvete.pizza, so Safe Cracker got its own subdomain:
safecracker.helvete.pizza
The production SvelteKit build runs through Node on:
127.0.0.1:3000
Apache sits in front of it as a reverse proxy.
Discord talks to Apache over HTTPS.
Apache talks to the local Node service.
The Node service talks to SQLite.
This project apparently needed architecture.
I created the DNS record.
Configured Apache virtual hosts.
Enabled the proxy modules.
Set up a separate Let’s Encrypt certificate using win-acme.
The certificate uses automatic filesystem HTTP validation so renewal does not require me to perform some ridiculous ceremonial DNS ritual every few months.
The Node application runs through a Windows Scheduled Task:
PGN Safe Cracker
It starts automatically with the server.
The production update process is now:
stop task
git pull
npm ci
npm run build
start task
There was also an educational period where I forgot the npm run build part.
Git had the new source.
Node was still happily running yesterday’s compiled application.
Computers are extremely literal.
The development copy also lives inside Dropbox, which repeatedly decided that locking generated Svelte files while I was trying to build them would be a helpful collaboration feature.
It was not.
I now pause Dropbox before Git or build operations.
We have reached an understanding.
Once the production app was stable, I added a health endpoint:
GET /api/health
It returns something like:
{
  "status": "ok",
  "safeNumber": 9,
  "date": "2026-09-21",
  "uptimeSeconds": 1843
}
Nothing sensitive.
Just enough information to prove:
Internet
→ Apache
→ Node
→ SvelteKit
→ daily-safe logic
is alive.
I tested it locally.
Then I tested the production URL.
It worked.
Tiny feature.
Extremely satisfying.
The Discord integration was still missing one thing, though.
If somebody was playing Safe Cracker, I wanted Discord to actually show that they were playing Safe Cracker.
So I added Rich Presence.
The Activity now updates Discord while you play.
It can show:
Cracking Safe #009
Playing the daily safe
with an elapsed timer.
Once the safe is open, it changes to something like:
Cracked Safe #009
19 guesses • 0:58 • 1 day streak
This required adding Discord’s:
rpc.activities.write
OAuth scope and keeping the Embedded App SDK instance alive after authentication so the rest of the game could update the Activity.
At first I thought the code was broken because absolutely nothing appeared on my profile.
After investigating the SDK, the scopes, the Activity state, and probably preparing myself emotionally for another authentication adventure, I discovered the problem.
Discord’s:
Share my activity
setting was turned off.
Turned it on.
There it was.
Of course.
The profile now shows Safe Cracker properly while I am playing, complete with the game artwork and current result.
That immediately led to the next feature.
If somebody cracks the safe, they should be able to brag about it.
So I added Discord’s native Activity sharing flow.
After completing the daily safe, there is now a:
SHARE RESULT
button.
It opens Discord’s normal share dialog and produces a proper result post.
Something like:
Shagwrath was playing Safe Cracker
🏆 Rank 1
🔥 2 Day Streak
27 Guesses • 01:09.12
Then Discord automatically attaches the Safe Cracker Activity card underneath it.
The card has the game artwork.
The game icon.
The Activity name.
And, most importantly, a big:
Play
button.
So someone can see another person’s score in Discord, click Play, and immediately launch the Activity themselves.
That little loop is probably my favorite thing in the project so far.
Someone plays.
Discord shows that they are playing.
They finish.
They share their score.
Someone else sees it.
They click Play.
Now they are trying to beat it.
That is exactly what I wanted this thing to feel like.
Safe Cracker currently has:
Discord OAuth authentication.
Secure persistent sessions.
A server-authoritative daily game.
Deterministic daily combinations.
SQLite persistence.
Resumable runs.
Server-controlled timing and attempts.
Completion lockout.
Current and best streaks.
Daily leaderboards.
A REST-style HTTP API.
A production health endpoint.
Apache reverse proxy hosting.
Automated HTTPS.
Windows startup through Scheduled Tasks.
GitHub deployment.
Discord Rich Presence.
Native Discord result sharing.
And a direct social path from:
Look at my score
to:
Fuck you, I can beat that.
Not bad for higher-or-lower.
The funniest part is that the visual design is still basically the prototype.
It is a dark rectangle.
There are buttons.
They work.
That was intentional.
I wanted to prove the entire game underneath the graphics before spending time decorating it.
Now I know that the authentication works.
The database works.
The API works.
The daily puzzle works.
Persistence works.
The leaderboard works.
Discord presence works.
Sharing works.
Production works.
So now I can finally start making the thing actually look and sound like Safe Cracker instead of a development interface somebody forgot to delete.
That will be a much nicer problem to have.
For now, though, I am extremely happy with what this little game quietly turned into.
I wanted to remake a number guessing game.
Instead I learned SvelteKit, built a server-authoritative web application, made an actual API, implemented OAuth and secure sessions, deployed a Node service behind Apache, added persistent multiplayer-adjacent statistics, and wired the whole thing directly into Discord.
Bucket list item:

Make an API.

Apparently checked.
Safe Cracker Discord Activity Home

updates/2026-09-23---a-little-bit-of-thi.content:
Cosmic Raven Records

Cosmic Raven Records Home
Some days are like this, you cant just focus on one thing, instead you bounce around from thing to thing.
A little progress in many things is better than no progress anywhere right? Whatever it takes to keep the momentum going.
It’s about time for another Cosmic Raven Records post, so I consulted my list of growing notes and ideas and then ignored them all and went to bed without doing anything. If it wasn’t for the last minute nothing would get done.
A few nights later when I was dozing off to sleep I was thinking about the Backrooms, new Horror, the infinite. It felt all very lovecraftian. I thought to myself that would be so cool if that’s the direction I was going here, and then it hit me. Well why not?
All the pieces are in place for my narrator to look into the void and the void look back, I had a long conversation with myself and tldr I realized that the project was telling me where to go, and this is where it wants to go next. It wasn’t about forcing it into a ‘cool’ direction, no, the story I’m telling is already about facing the infinite and why not explore that even deeper.
I don’t want to give the story away, for multiple reasons, but my clear direction is even clearer and I see, with confidence, my ability to do the things I want with the story without compromising it.
And along the way I will make sure the story is being told, they way it needs to be told.
Safe Cracker Discord Activity
Safe Cracker Discord Activity Home
I have made great progress, all that remains is the art, sound and Discord approval.
I know the art will take time but I want to finish it now! I am so close to finish I am already salivating at the possibilities for new projects. Because working on 5 things all at once is a total sane person thing to do.
Warren Buffet has that thing about make a list of the most important things to you to work on, then do those before moving on. I guess I missed the part where you’re not supposed to do them all at once.
I did some mocks, started the different screens, got the connecting screen working.


Then I made a palette.
Order of operations, gah!
So now I will remake the connection screen and redo my work on the main screen, but hey, its progress!
Maybe I’ll just go play Marvel Rivals…

updates/2026-09-24---another-mix-bag-sor.content:
Safe Cracker Discord Activity

Safe Cracker Discord Activity Home
At least I am consistent. I worked on the same 2 projects 2 days in a row now.
I really want to finish up the GUI assets for the Safe Cracker Discord Activity Home but making the safe/vault element was hard. Lot’s of wasted time, but the end results we’re worth the struggle. I am really happy with how it turned out.
Now I can finish up the rest of the test and visual layout, and hopefully I’ll have that all wired into the actual app by the end of this weekend!
Next is music and SFX, I am expecting to do those quickly so of course that will take another week I am sure.
Future Planning
In the meantime there are plenty of other projects on my mind.

updates/2026-09-26.2---i-accidentally-be.title: 2026-09-26 - I Accidentally Became A Dune Server Goblin
updates/2026-09-26.2---i-accidentally-be.content:
I Accidentally Became A Dune Server Goblin
This started because I wanted a private Dune server.
That seems simple enough.
Install the dedicated server.
Set a password.
Invite friends.
Run around Arrakis.
Try not to get eaten by the worm.
Naturally, I ended up learning about SteamCMD, Hyper-V networking, Windows NAT, Kubernetes pods, container images, UDP port ranges, memory limits, broken upstream builds, and the emotional burden of naming an internal switch Bootyhole.
This happens to me a lot.
The server is for Dune: Awakening, which has a self-hosted server tool.
The normal game is Steam app:
1172710
The self-hosted server tool is:
4754530
That distinction matters because the first rule of running a dedicated server is apparently:

Make sure you are installing the server.

Inspiring.
The install itself lives on my dedicated Windows server.
I already use this machine for other nonsense, because apparently I have decided that “fun hobby” means “becoming my own underpaid infrastructure department.”
The Dune server went into:
C:\PGN\DUNE
SteamCMD went into:
C:\PGN\STEAMCMD
I learned very quickly to avoid cute folder names with brackets.
Something like:
C:\[PGN]\[DUNE]
looks organized until PowerShell and scripts start treating brackets like they are part of an ancient curse. Thanks Multi Theft Auto.
So now it is boring paths only.
Boring paths are beautiful.
The first big wall was networking.
The server runs inside a self-hosting VM, and my first instinct was basically:
Make VM.
Give VM internet.
Profit.
Unfortunately, OVH dedicated servers and Hyper-V bridged networking do not care about my instincts.
The VM was alive.
The host was alive.
The network was allegedly alive.
The server was not meaningfully reachable.
The clean solution ended up being an internal Hyper-V switch with Windows NAT.
The working switch is named:
Bootyhole
I will not be taking questions at this time.
The VM sits at:
192.168.69.69
because if I am already debugging haunted UDP traffic on a private Arrakis server, I am at least going to entertain myself.
The final network path is:
Internet
→ Windows Server
→ Windows Firewall
→ Windows NAT
→ Hyper-V Internal Switch
→ Dune VM
→ Kubernetes
→ Dune game server pods
That is a lot of arrows for “play video game with friends.”
The official ports were not the whole story either.
The obvious range was:
7777-7810 UDP
plus:
31982 TCP
But the setup did not fully behave until we also forwarded the inter-server gateway range:
7888-7921 UDP
Before that, the server could get weirdly close to working.
Visible enough to taunt me.
Not connected enough to play.
That is worse than simply being broken.
A server that is completely broken is honest.
A server that appears in the browser and then refuses to connect is a butthead.
Eventually, the network behaved.
The server appeared.
The password prompt worked.
I could join.
Victory.
For about five minutes.
Then came tuning.
The Dune self-hosting setup uses config files named:
UserEngine.ini
UserGame.ini
These apply across the battlegroup unless you override things per server in the battlegroup editor.
I set the server name.
I set the password.
I played with mining multipliers.
I looked at sandstorms, worms, deterioration, PvP zones, land claim settings, all the usual private server temptations.
You start with:

I just want a chill server for friends.

Then ten minutes later you are staring at:
Vehicle.SandwormInvulnerabilitySecondsOnServerRestart=7200.0
like some kind of discount Arrakis systems administrator.
At one point I wanted to enter a special area and the server just refused.
This turned out to be a memory limit issue.
The pod for that area had been getting:
OOMKilled
Exit Code 137
It had a 5Gi memory limit.
I gave it more memory, restarted the battlegroup, and it worked.
That one was satisfying because it was a real problem with a real answer.
Area broken.
Pod killed for memory.
Increase memory.
Area works.
Beautiful.
Computers almost never give you that kind of clean emotional closure.
Then the server disappeared.
I logged in one morning and did not see my server in the list.
The battlegroup status screen was also suspicious.
The infrastructure looked fine.
Database? Fine.
Gateway? Fine.
Director? Fine.
But the actual game server rows were blank.
No map names.
No phase.
No useful status.
That is when things became less “private server setup” and more “I am reading Kubernetes entrails at breakfast.”
Inside the VM, the real battlegroup namespace was:
funcom-seabass-sh-238803c537a22e2-fdofyf
There was also a second, unused battlegroup namespace:
funcom-seabass-sh-238803c537a22e2-krmfhh
That second one later got deleted, but at this stage I did not want to touch anything until I knew which pile of letters contained my actual world.
The real one was fdofyf.
I checked the pods.
The infrastructure pods were running.
The actual playable servers were not.
Overmap and Survival were both in:
CrashLoopBackOff
The describe output showed:
Exit Code 139
That is not a happy exit code.
The previous logs had the real clue:
Failed to load data table property 'm_SpiceFieldTypeDataTable'
and:
/Game/Dune/Systems/SpiceHarvesting/DT_SpiceFieldTypes
Then the server caught:
Signal 11
and fell over.
So the game server was trying to load a Spice Harvesting data table that was not there.
Which, for a Dune game, feels like a pretty unfortunate thing to misplace.
I checked my config files.
Nothing.
No SpiceHarvesting.
No DT_SpiceFieldTypes.
No m_SpiceFieldTypeDataTable.
I searched /home/dune.
I searched /funcom.
I checked disk space.
Disk was fine.
The bad path was not in my visible config.
So naturally I did the ancient ritual:
Maybe update fixes it.
It did not.
At first, the update just re-applied the same build:
2007976-0-shipping
I removed and reimported the game server container image.
Still broken.
The same crash.
The same missing Spice table.
The same blank status rows.
At that point, the evidence was pretty clear:
This was not my network.
This was not my ports.
This was not my config.
This was not disk space.
This was not the VM being haunted.
Funcom had pushed a bad self-host build.
Honestly, that was kind of a relief.
It is annoying when something is broken upstream, but it is also nice to stop gaslighting yourself with port forwarding rules.
I sent an email through the Funcom site.
Discord pointed me that way.
Eventually, Funcom fixed the build.
It did not fix itself automatically.
A normal restart did not fix it.
I had to run the server update again, pull the corrected build, and restart the battlegroup.
Then everything came back.
Actual game rows.
Actual status.
Actual server visibility.
Actual joy.
Once the real server was healthy, I cleaned up the unused battlegroup.
The dead one was:
sh-238803c537a22e2-krmfhh
It had no resources, no useful running server, and no future except confusing me later.
So I deleted its namespace.
The real one remains:
sh-238803c537a22e2-fdofyf
That is the world.
Do not delete the world.
That should probably be written on a sticky note above the server.
This project now has a proper doomsday guide because there is absolutely no chance I am rediscovering all of this from scratch six months from now.
The guide covers:
SteamCMD
Dune app IDs
Hyper-V setup
Windows NAT
Firewall rules
Required port ranges
Battlegroup setup
UserGame.ini
UserEngine.ini
Backups
Kubernetes commands
CrashLoopBackOff troubleshooting
OOMKilled fixes
Bad Funcom build symptoms
Deleting unused battlegroups safely
Basically everything future me needs when something explodes and present me is not around to explain why the private switch is called Bootyhole.
What did I learn?
I learned that self-hosting modern games is not just “run server.exe.”
It is a stack.
A weird stack.
A Windows host runs a Linux VM that runs Kubernetes that runs containers that run the game servers that talk through gateways that depend on RabbitMQ and a database and a director and a handful of UDP ports that all need to agree about reality.
That sentence is exhausting.
I also learned that a server can be broken in at least six completely different ways:
Wrong Steam app
Bad install path
Bad VM networking
Missing NAT mapping
Low memory limit
Bad upstream build
And each one looks like:
Server no work
Very helpful.
But now it works.
The server is up.
The bad battlegroup is gone.
The network setup is documented.
The weird Funcom build failure is documented.
The recovery path is documented.
And most importantly:
Bootyhole lives.
Not bad for wanting to play Dune with friends.
Dune Private Server Doomsday Guide
Dune Private Server Home

updates/2026-09-26.3---i-swear-i'm-going.filePath: Updates/2026-09-26.3 - I Swear I'm Going to Finish This Game!.md
updates/2026-09-26.3---i-swear-i'm-going.title: 2026-09-26.3 - I Swear I'm Going to Finish This Game!
updates/2026-09-26.3---i-swear-i'm-going.content:
I am making an actual Game Boy game.
Not a modern game that looks vaguely green.
Not a Unity game with a pixel filter.
An actual .gb ROM that runs on a Game Boy, is built with GBDK, has to fit into ROM banks, uses the Game Boy sound hardware, and can become a real cartridge if I ever finish the damn thing.
The game is called:
Garth's Game DMG

It is a virtual pet game about Garth Algar.
Garth lives in a little industrial spaceship room, eats terrible food, plays games, sleeps, talks in a horrible little robot voice, tells jokes, and now has a growing gas problem that the player will have to manage.
Video games are art.
The project started much smaller than that.
The first goal was basically:
Put text on the screen.

I had a GBDK project in:
C:\gbdk\examples\gb\garth_game_i
and I wanted to learn what I was doing instead of having an entire game dumped in front of me all at once.
So it started with a splash screen, some centered text, and a little menu.
Then I pressed Up and Down and the menu scrolled up the screen and duplicated itself.
Great start.
The problem was that I was clearing and redrawing the console like it was a normal terminal. The Game Boy did not agree with my interpretation of events.
That became one of the recurring themes of the project.
I would look at something and think:

This should be simple.

And the Game Boy would respond:

You have misunderstood tiles.

The splash screen briefly appeared scrambled while VRAM was loading, so I learned to turn the display off, load everything, and turn it back on.
I made food icons out of groups of 8×8 sprites and discovered that converted tiles do not necessarily stay in the order I imagined they would.
The food was jumbled.
Then it was differently jumbled.
Then pieces of the previous food stayed behind like some kind of haunted hamburger.
Eventually the food assets were split up, rebuilt, arranged into controlled quadrants, and made to behave.
That was around the point where this stopped being a test and started becoming a game.
Garth got three persistent needs:
FOOD
FUN
POWER
They decrease over time.
The player maintains them by playing short minigames, and those minigames also feed a progression system that gradually raises the maximum value of each stat.
The starting cap is 30.
With enough activities, elapsed days, and good care, a stat can unlock another ten points at a time until it reaches 100.
When that happens the game displays:
MAXIMUM UP!

It also saves all of this to SRAM.
That meant adding CONTINUE, NEW GAME, save validation, and an overwrite warning so one careless button press did not murder Garth’s entire history.
The first minigame was feeding him.
There are four food slots. Each slot cycles through pieces of ten different foods and the player stops them one at a time.
If all four match, it is Perfect.
Three and one is Tasty.
Two and two is Unique.
Everything else is Sloppy.
The game then invents a name for whatever biological incident the player created.
A perfect food is easy.
A mixed burger and pizza can become something like a Bizza or a Purgizza.
Failure can produce:
SLOPPY SNACK

which feels less like a result and more like a threat.
The second game became a button-matching game.
The third has the player move a little catcher across the bottom of the screen, catching falling Zs and avoiding exclamation points so Garth can get some sleep.
At this point the game had a real care loop.
Feed him.
Play with him.
Help him sleep.
Watch his mood change.
Save the game and come back later.
Then I taught him to talk.
I did not use recorded samples.
I made a tiny speech system called Lang808 that breaks dialogue into letter-like sound tokens and plays them through the Game Boy audio hardware.
There are vowel sounds, consonant sounds, punctuation pauses, and timing rules.
It is not exactly speech.
It is the sound of a Game Boy being haunted by somebody who would like to tell you something.
Perfect for Garth.
His face animates while he talks, but that created another fun problem where changing the animation frame could restart the speech.
So he would begin a sentence, move his face, and apparently decide to begin the sentence again.
Later the sound could get stuck when leaving the screen, so the stop routine had to explicitly shut the channels down.
Then the dialogue grew large enough that it had to be split across ROM banks.
Then accessing the wrong thing from the wrong bank could produce a mostly white screen and trap me in TALK mode.
Normal game-development stuff.
Music came next.
The game now has menu music, four mood themes, three minigame songs, result music, synthesized speech, and sound effects.
The music uses hUGEDriver and lives in Bank 4.
The sound effects needed their own channel, which meant removing stray commands from that channel in the music exports.
And because the minigames use their own blocking loops, every one of those loops has to update the music driver itself or the song starts and then freezes.
That was a weird one.
The code says the music is playing.
The Game Boy says:

No it isn’t.

Memory has been an adventure too.
At one point ROM0 was 98% full with 341 bytes remaining.
Later banking work improved that, but the more recent builds still had ROM0 around 96–97% and the music bank around 90%.
Those are not numbers that inspire calm.
The Game Boy can absolutely do a lot, but it expects you to know exactly where everything lives.
Code can be in one bank.
Data can be in another.
The screen has its own tile memory.
Sprites have their own rules.
And if two screens both decide tile 211 belongs to them, the Game Boy does not schedule a meeting to resolve the conflict.
It simply corrupts one of them.
That happened with the randomized menu backgrounds. The menu looked fine until I visited the pet screen and came back, at which point some of the background styles were garbage.
The pet UI was overwriting part of the menu’s tile range.
The fix was to reload all sixteen menu tiles every time the menu is shown.
Simple once you know what is happening.
Several hours less simple before that.
Eventually the game reached a point where the major systems worked.
The pet stats worked.
Saving worked.
Progression worked.
The three minigames worked.
Dialogue, face animation, speech, music, and sound effects worked.
I playtested it for a while and got feedback from other people.
And then I had the extremely convenient realization that I wanted to redesign almost every major screen in the game.
The current build is a good game-shaped machine.
The redesign is about making it look and feel like something I would actually want to buy.
The new home screen is a detailed little cabin.
Garth stands in the room and will have different animations depending on his mood.
Four stat bars sit across the top-right.
The bottom of the screen has icons for four minigames, a joke button, TALK mode, and a mood indicator.
And yes, there are now four stats.
FOOD
FUN
POWER
GAS
GAS works backwards from the others.
FOOD, FUN, and POWER are better when they are high and slowly decrease over time.
GAS is better when it is low and slowly increases over time.
Eating will make it increase faster or give it an immediate bump.
Eventually Garth has to release the pressure.
Which brings us to the fourth minigame.
The existing games are also getting actual names and a shared three-part structure:
TITLE ANIMATION
GAME
RESULTS
The food game is now:
FOOD IS GOOD

The button game is:
SIMON SAYS

The nap game remains:
CATCH SOME ZS

And the gas game is:
PASS THE GAS

The Pass the Gas title sequence currently goes:
black screen
OOPSIE POOPSIE
black screen
WHOOPS POOPS
black screen
PASS THE GAS
This may be the best thing I have ever designed.
The play screen is an industrial pressure-control room with a huge bubbling tank in the center.
There are separate meters for burp pressure and fart pressure.
The controls are:
A: BURP
B: FART
The exact game mechanic is still being worked out.
It may be a pressure-balancing game.
It may involve alternating the two releases.
It may involve some amount of button mashing.
The important thing is that the art has tremendous fart energy and I do not want to waste it on a bad game.
The other new screens have the same kind of oversized personality.
Food Is Good takes place inside a ridiculous food machine.
Simon Says has six large Game Boy button symbols and seven result lights.
Catch Some Zs now happens in space, with huge falling Zs, a bigger catcher, planets, stars, and the score shoved into the footer so the playfield can breathe.
The new images are mockups right now.
They still have to be broken into reusable 8×8 tiles, assigned to ROM banks, converted into Game Boy assets, and adjusted whenever the hardware tells me I have been too optimistic.
Some of them will change.
They have to.
But the direction finally feels right.
This is no longer just:

Look, I made a virtual pet on a Game Boy.

I want it to become:

Oh wow. I want that cartridge.

That is the finish line now.
A real ROM.
A real cartridge.
A label.
A box.
A manual.
Something that feels like it escaped from an alternate version of the 1990s where somebody approved a virtual pet game about a strange little man managing his food, mood, sleep, and internal gas pressure.
The current working game is the foundation.
The new home screen and minigames are the next enormous step.
I have already made the source archive, technical notes, game design document, roadmap, and enough documentation that Future Me should at least be able to identify the wreckage.
Now I just have to fit the new game into the Game Boy.
Easy.
Cosmic Raven Universe
Garth Algar
Garths Game DMG Home

Garth’s Game I - Technical Design

updates/2026-09-27.1---i-gave-shag's-lab.content:
9.27.2026 - I Gave Shag’s Lab a Tune-Up
Today was mostly a cleanup day for Shag’s Lab.
The site has been working, but the vault has grown enough that some of the little inconsistencies were starting to matter. Different project names, empty properties, status values that did not quite mean the same thing, a few weird folder names, and some pages that were technically public even though they were still empty.
So I finally sat down and cleaned the whole thing up.
The biggest change was adding a new page type:
type: project-parent
This is for things that are not really projects themselves, but are containers for multiple projects.
For example, Keychron C100 is now a parent, while things like Keychron C100 Custom Firmware and Keychron C100 Custom Keycaps are the actual projects underneath it.
The same idea now works for things like Instruments and My Mini Retro Television.
That already makes the Explorer feel a lot more sane.
I also went through the metadata across the vault and standardized the headers. Projects now have consistent project names and statuses, empty placeholder properties were removed, Wiki pages were cleaned up, a few old project names were normalized, and some accidental copy/paste nonsense got fixed.
There were, naturally, a couple casualties.
Two Teenage Engineering synth folders got mangled by an encoding problem during the cleanup and briefly showed up twice in the website Explorer with names like:
EPâ€“40
Very futuristic.
Those were cleaned up too, and the new metadata validator actually caught the problem before one of the broken versions could quietly become part of the site.
That validator is probably one of my favorite changes from today.
The publishing script now checks the vault before Quartz builds and complains if I do something stupid like:

forget a required project name
use an invalid status
mismatch an update date
publish an empty page
create inconsistent project metadata

That means Shag’s Lab is getting to the point where the tooling is starting to protect the structure instead of me having to remember every rule manually.
I also added a Wiki section, which I have wanted from the beginning. It is still pretty sparse, but now there is a real place for notes that are not projects or chronological updates.
Oh, and the website finally has a visitor counter.
Nothing ridiculous. Just:
Shag's Lab · 5 visitors
Nice and boring.
There are still a few things I want to revisit later:

sort projects more intentionally by status
formally define what every status means
keep improving the parent/project hierarchy
clean up old broken/private links
make an actual good Shag’s Lab logo

But the important part is that the site feels a lot less like a pile of Markdown files now.
It is starting to feel like an actual little system.
Which was kind of the whole point.

updates/2026-09-27.2---i-accidentally-do.title: 2026-09-27.2 - I Accidentally Downloaded 131GB of Television
updates/2026-09-27.2---i-accidentally-do.content:
I Accidentally Downloaded 131GB of Television
Last time I wrote about this project I had figured out how to make my tiny retro television play custom videos from USB drives.
That was the important breakthrough.
The USB drives could be little cartridges.
Not just one show per drive either.
I wanted fake television stations.
Nickelodeon.
Cartoon Network.
Kids’ WB.
Fox Kids.
Sci-Fi.
UPN.
HBO.
AMC.
Twenty little 4GB flash drives pretending to be cable television.
At the end of the last update I had one problem.
I needed commercials.
A lot of commercials.
Because this:
Rugrats
Hey Arnold!
CatDog
Doug
is a playlist.
This:
Rugrats
Fruit Roll-Ups commercial
Hey Arnold!
Nintendo commercial
CatDog
Pizza Hut commercial
Doug
PSA
is television.
So I started collecting old commercials.
This got out of hand almost immediately.
I found a few Internet Archive collections with individually clipped 90s commercials, giant collections of general American TV commercials, old Nickelodeon and Cartoon Network recordings, late-night stuff, promos, bumpers, and whatever else people had rescued from VHS tapes over the years.
At first I thought I would just grab maybe 120 or 150 commercials.
That was adorable.
The first commercial library ended up with hundreds of candidates.
And then I discovered the real problem.
I had to actually look at them.
There is apparently no useful way to look at a directory containing hundreds of files named things like:
commercial_103.mp4
BK_1997_02.mp4
nick_break_4.mp4
and decide which ones belong on fake Nickelodeon without slowly losing your mind.
So naturally I made a tool.
I wrote a PowerShell scanner that walks the archive, calls ffprobe, and records things like:
duration
video codec
audio codec
resolution
frame rate
sample rate
year
source collection
filename
It also tries to tell the difference between an individual commercial, a short break, a bumper, and a giant source recording.
That gave me a CSV.
Which was better.
But I still had hundreds of video files to review.
So then I made another tool.
The second script generates thumbnails with FFmpeg and builds a local HTML review site.
Now instead of opening random files in VLC one at a time, I get a giant wall of old television garbage.
Perfect.
Every clip has a thumbnail, filename, duration, source, preview button, category dropdown, and notes field.
I can tag things as:
KIDS_90S
KIDS_00S
GENERAL_90S
GENERAL_00S
LATE_NIGHT
PSA
PROMO
BUMPER
IDENT
NEEDS_CLIPPED
SKIP
The browser saves my progress locally and I can export the finished curation to CSV.
This is one of those little side tools that probably took longer to build than just suffering through the files manually once.
But now I can do this forever.
Which is much more dangerous.
The first review pass had 411 logical assets.
I reviewed every single one.
The final pile included:
102 KIDS_90S
40  GENERAL_90S
7   GENERAL_00S
11  LATE_NIGHT
10  PSA
48  PROMO
15  BUMPER
1   IDENT
8   NEEDS_CLIPPED
169 SKIP
That was already enough to make the 90s carts pretty convincing.
But there was a very obvious hole.
The early 2000s.
I had almost nothing.
So I found another collection called Commercials (Clean).
It contains almost two thousand commercials covering roughly 2000 through 2015.
The uploader had already trimmed and cleaned a lot of them, which is exactly what I needed.
I scanned that too.
There were hundreds of commercials just from 2000 through 2002.
I absolutely did not want to review another two thousand videos.
So I made a second version of the review page that only showed early-2000s individual-commercial-length clips.
It also had its own browser storage so I could not accidentally destroy the first finished review.
That would have been a very funny way to lose several hours of my life.
The new collection looked terrible at first.
After 76 clips I had only found 9 kid commercials.
I thought I had downloaded 20GB of insurance companies and SUVs.
Then it suddenly got good.
I stopped at 193 reviewed clips with:
89 KIDS_00S
95 GENERAL_00S
2  PSA
7  SKIP
There are still 449 clips sitting there unreviewed.
I am leaving them that way on purpose.
I do not want to reuse commercials on the finished cartridges if I can avoid it, so that unreviewed pile is now reserve ammunition.
If I start running out later, I already know where to go.
At this point the commercial problem is basically solved.
Which meant it was time to move on to the thing that will probably make the fake channels feel even more convincing than the commercials.
Bumpers.
Idents.
“We’ll be right back.”
“Now back to the show.”
“Up next.”
Station IDs.
Little five-second pieces of television that nobody really thinks about until they disappear.
I was originally planning to hunt those down one network at a time.
Then I found a giant community collection of already-clipped bumpers.
And another archive.
And another.
I decided to keep this phase USA-only for now.
There are some fantastic Canadian YTV and Teletoon archives out there, but if I keep expanding the scope every time I find something cool, this television is eventually going to contain the entire history of broadcasting.
So I downloaded the American stuff.
Then I ran an inventory.
The folder is now about:
131 GB
14,414 files
I have accidentally built a television archive.
The really useful branding collections alone contain more than five thousand files.
One of them has folders with roughly:
1,700+ Cartoon Network bumpers
800+  Adult Swim clips
700+  Toonami clips
300+  Nickelodeon bumpers
200+  Fox Kids clips
100+  MTV bumpers
60+   Nick GAS clips
There is also SNICK material.
Kids’ WB.
Cartoon Cartoon Fridays.
Cartoon Network Groovies.
Show-specific bumpers.
“Now back” bumpers.
“Up next” clips.
Promos.
Station IDs.
All kinds of weird little pieces of dead television infrastructure.
This is fantastic.
It also means I do not need to manually cut all of this stuff out of three-hour VHS recordings.
A lot of it is already separated and named.
Eventually I will make another review tool for this pile too.
The filenames are structured well enough that I should be able to auto-classify a lot of it into things like:
NETWORK
 
NICK
SNICK
CN
KWB
FOX
TOONAMI
ADULT_SWIM
MTV
NICK_GAS
and:
TYPE
 
IDENT
BUMPER_IN
BUMPER_OUT
NEXT
PROMO
INTRO
SIGN_OFF
OTHER
Then I can just preview the good candidates and keep the ones that fit the stations I am building.
The ridiculous part is that downloading all of this also created several future stations almost by accident.
I now have enough Toonami material that a Toonami cartridge seems inevitable.
Same with Adult Swim.
MTV is suddenly possible.
Nick GAS is sitting there asking questions.
I am trying very hard not to order more flash drives.
For now.
The project is in a really good place to stop for a few days.
The hardware works.
USB cartridges work.
I know the encoding format the television likes.
The twenty-cart lineup exists.
The episode manifests exist.
The 90s commercial library is curated.
The early-2000s commercial library is curated enough to use.
There is a giant reserve pool if I ever need more commercials.
And I now have more station branding than I know what to do with.
The next major step will be turning all of these ingredients into an actual automated cart builder.
Something that can take:
station
episode list
commercial pool
bumpers
idents
and spit out a numbered, correctly encoded fake television broadcast that fits on one of the 4GB drives.
Then I can finally stop building infrastructure for fake television and actually watch fake television.
Probably.
I started this project because I wanted to put different videos on a novelty TV.
I now have 131GB of archival television infrastructure.
This seems proportionate.
My Mini Retro Television Channels Home

updates/2026-09-28---i-downloaded-ten-ye.title: 2026-09-28 - I Downloaded Ten Years of Discord and Accidentally Became the Clan Historian
updates/2026-09-28---i-downloaded-ten-ye.content:
I Downloaded Ten Years of Discord and Accidentally Became the Clan Historian
This started because I had a stupid thought:
Can I just… download the entire history of my Discord server?
Turns out, yes.
And once I realized that, obviously the next reasonable thing to do was dump roughly a decade of my friends’ conversations into a pile of JSON and start doing archaeology on it.
The Discord server is for PGN — Progeny Gaming Network, which has existed in one form or another since around 2015. We started as more of a traditional gaming clan around stuff like Multi Theft Auto and Minecraft, but over the years it slowly turned into something much harder to define.
At this point PGN is basically:

a gaming group
a pile of old dedicated servers
a graveyard full of games we swear we’re going to play again
a software lab
an excuse for me to host things
and, mostly, a group of friends who somehow never completely logged out

So I decided I wanted the receipts.
Step One: Vacuum Up Discord
I set up a dedicated Discord bot and used DiscordChatExporter to export the entire server.
I did the archive in JSON first because I was less interested in having a pretty offline copy of Discord and more interested in having data I could actually do things with.
The first complete archive came out to:

79 JSON channel/thread exports
68,975 unique messages
almost exactly 10 years of Discord history
earliest surviving message: October 19, 2016
latest message in the export: September 27, 2026

There are also thousands of attachment and embed references waiting for me to deal with later.
The raw text archive is only around 30 MB compressed, which is honestly kind of hilarious considering how much human nonsense is contained inside it.
The first message in the surviving archive is:

Harro

Which is about as dignified a beginning as PGN deserves.
Step Two: Apparently We’re Doing Data Archaeology Now
Once I had the JSON, staring at 69,000 messages one at a time sounded like a terrible idea.
So I started building a little analysis tool I called:
PGN Discord Archaeologist
The first version normalizes the exported messages and generates things like:

yearly and monthly activity
channel statistics
member activity
game/thread timelines
Steam links
long-term participation
attachment counts
return-after-disappearing patterns
and candidates for stupid clan titles

It also builds a SQLite database so the archive becomes something I can actually search.
That means instead of scrolling through Discord for two hours trying to remember something, I can eventually ask questions like:

When did we first start playing PUBG?


When did Dargeath disappear?


How many separate times did we revive Crossout?


When did Helvete become a restaurant?


Who disappeared for four years and then randomly came back?

These are important historical questions.
Step Three: Oh No, There’s Actually A Story Here
The funniest part was that the archive stopped looking like a pile of chat logs pretty quickly.
There are very obvious eras.
2017 is absolutely enormous. It is by far the busiest year in the archive.
Then there are periods where everybody piles into ARK, PUBG, Crossout, Grounded, Valheim, Helldivers, Minecraft, The Isle, Dune, or whatever terrible multiplayer decision we have made that month.
But underneath all of that there is a much more interesting pattern.
PGN keeps doing the same thing on different technology.
Early on it was:

Let’s run an MTA server.

Then:

Let’s run a Minecraft server.

Then:

Let’s run an ARK server.

Then:

Okay but can we mod the server?

Then:

Can we write our own scripts?

Then:

Maybe we should just make games.

Then:

Maybe this twenty-year-old Battlefront game needs a website, persistent player identities, statistics, XP, achievements, an economy, Discord integration, and a database.

You know.
Normal progression.
One of the best lines I found in the archive was Steven describing old game communities in 2022:

a place to interact with a community, the game being the medium

That might actually be the best explanation of PGN I’ve ever heard.
The games keep changing.
The group is the thing that survives them.
The Things That Refuse To Die
There are also a few things that keep resurfacing over and over again.
Helvete
Helvete predates PGN and originally comes out of the old MTA era.
Over the years it has been:

an old gang/group
a logo
a possible PGN rebrand
a revived SAES group
a motorcycle club
a restaurant
a fast-food joke
and now the name behind helvete.pizza

At this point Helvete is less of a specific organization and more like some kind of cursed cultural object we keep carrying from game to game.
Dargeath
Dargeath was our old Minecraft RPG server.
At one point I went looking for the backups and realized they were probably gone.
The Discord archive literally contains:

rip Dargeath

Naturally, this did not stop us from trying to resurrect it repeatedly.
There is now a thread called Dargeath 17.0.
Death is apparently a temporary status.
Safe Cracker
Safe Cracker might be my favorite example.
It started life as a little safe-cracking concept tied to the old MTA/SAES days.
Then I rebuilt it in Unity.
Then I considered making it a Game Boy game because apparently I enjoy suffering.
Then it became a Steam game.
Now I’m turning it into a Discord Activity.
At this rate I expect to be porting Safe Cracker to a refrigerator in 2031.
Then I Wrote The History Book
Once I realized there was an actual narrative hiding in the archive, I stopped treating this as purely a statistics project.
I started reconstructing a proper history of PGN.
The first version was around 7,000 words.
Then I went back into the archive and did a much deeper pass.
The current internal version is about 9,500 words, backed by 86 individual historical events pulled directly from the archive.
For each major event I keep:

the date
channel
author
Discord message ID
original excerpt
and a short note explaining why it matters

That distinction is important because PGN has now existed long enough that we have actual oral history.
People remember things.
People also remember things incorrectly.
So I started separating:
documented event
from:
later recollection
from:
clan mythology
For example, we have a later song that describes the lineage as:
Hell Soldiers → Helvete → WSS → PGN
That is absolutely part of PGN lore.
But until I dig up older records, I’m treating it as oral history rather than pretending I found a 2013 board meeting transcript.
This is apparently the level of archival rigor I am bringing to a gaming clan whose Battlefront server is named:
PGN - Ewok Around and Find Out
The Discord Is Becoming A Museum
Something else became obvious while doing this.
The modern PGN server itself has slowly started preserving history.
We now have things like:

dedicated project channels
game threads
server status posts
The Workshop
an About PGN page
and an actual Graveyard category for dead games and projects

Older PGN history is incredibly difficult to reconstruct because almost everything happened in one giant #general channel, voice chat, game servers, or services that no longer exist.
Modern PGN leaves ruins with signs on them.
That is much easier for the archaeologist.
The Perfect Ending
There is one detail I could not have planned better.
The archive ends on September 27, 2026.
The final message in the entire exported history is an automated Discord welcome message.
It says:

Welcome to Progeny Gaming Network, @PGN Archivist!

The bot I created to preserve the history became the last event preserved by the first archive.
That is so absurdly appropriate that if I wrote it into a story I would probably think it was too cute.
But that’s actually how the export ends.
What’s Next
The text history is only the first layer.
There are still thousands of attachments, screenshots, embeds, logos, maps, project images, memes, and probably completely forgotten artifacts referenced in the archive.
So the next obvious terrible idea is to start indexing those too.
Eventually I want this to become something closer to a little PGN digital museum:

a proper timeline
game eras
old servers
project histories
member timelines
screenshots
old logos
running jokes
ridiculous quotes
dead projects
resurrected dead projects
and a Hall of Titles

The Hall of Titles is especially important.
Things like:

The Ancient One
The Chronicler
The Server Goblin
Return From the Void
The Necromancer
The Ping Lord
and, obviously, Clan Troll

I can use the archive to produce candidates based on actual evidence.
Then I can post the nominations in Discord and let everyone fight over them.
Which is probably the most historically accurate way possible to decide anything about PGN.
For now, though, I have something I never really expected to have:
a ten-year primary-source archive of one very weird group of friends.
And for once, when one of our projects inevitably dies, I might actually remember what the hell happened.

wiki/multi-theft-auto.title: Multi Theft Auto
wiki/multi-theft-auto.content:
My personal involvement with Multi Theft auto start in 2014 on the San Andreas Emergency Services Server, SAES:RPG.
After Hell’s Soldiers and making Helvete, I had a falling out with the SAES clan, and left to join some friends on the Why So Serious RPG server.
After another falling out there me and some other friends left to make Progeny Gaming Network and the PGN RPG server, and another group of people went out to make Nightlife RPG, then Excision, then Nightlife RPG again. Then we got back together during covid to make ANAL RPG, not my finest name choice but I am proud of what we did.
I have worked on a few other servers, including SGN RPG and DBZS Zombie Survival RPG, boy I am getting tired of typing RPG.

index.content:
Welcome to my Lab.
This is part blog, part wiki. All me.
Browse Updates Home to see what I am currently working or wondering on.
Projects Home contains a list of my long running projects, and all the information therein.
Wiki Home is where I keep articles, definitions, history, and other rabbit holes that do not really belong to a single project.
Whatever it is you’re looking for I hope you can find it here or at least find something interesting I have done to inspire you.
